title: Is the World Getting Smaller? Network-Driven Heterogeneity in Gravity-Model Elasticities
author:
  - name: Zsolt T. Kosztyán
    email: kosztyan.zsolt@gtk.uni-pannon.hu
    affiliation: Department of Quantitative Methods, University of Pannonia
  - name: Rita Mátrai

abstract: |
  Gravity models constitute the workhorse of empirical international trade research, yet the temporal stability of their core parameters---distance and GDP elasticities---remains underexplored, particularly in relation to the evolving structure of trade networks. This study investigates the bidirectional Granger-causal relationships between gravity model coefficients and trade network topology using two complementary databases: the OECD Inter-Country Input-Output tables (1995--2020, 45 sectors) and the CEPII-BACI bilateral trade database (1995--2022, 97 product groups). We employ three methodologically distinct causality testing approaches---traditional panel Granger tests, Bayesian model comparison via Bayes factors, and Random Forest-based variable importance analysis---to establish robust directional relationships while accounting for potential nonlinearities. A key methodological innovation is the incorporation of fractal dimensions and local lacunarity distribution moments (mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis) as novel network indicators capturing multiscale heterogeneity, alongside conventional centrality and modularity measures. Using network-based dimensionality reduction (Generalized Network-based Dimensionality Analysis), we identify two to four distinct temporal clusters of sectors and products exhibiting heterogeneous gravity coefficient dynamics, with forecasts extended to 2030 using Bayesian ARIMA models. Our results reveal significant Granger-causal relationships between network structural properties and gravity coefficients, but the three methods diverge sharply in how much structure they detect: the Random Forest approach identifies three- to four-fold more significant sector-and product-level relationships than the two linear methods. At the aggregate level, centralization measures and heterogeneity indicators (lacunarity, fractal dimension) Granger-precede GDP elasticities broadly and consistently across sectors and products, whereas their relationship with distance elasticity is concentrated in specific sectors and product groups rather than operating uniformly across the aggregate network. Distance elasticity shows declining magnitude over the study period at the aggregate level, but substantial heterogeneity persists across product groups, with some clusters exhibiting stable or even increasing distance sensitivity. The cross-database triangulation confirms that these patterns are robust to alternative trade flow conceptualizations (gross vs. value-added trade). These findings contribute to international trade theory in three ways. First, they provide systematic evidence of temporal precedence -- established via Granger-style tests, not structural causal identification -- showing that the extensive margin of trade---captured by network topology---consistently leads the intensive margin reflected in gravity coefficients, consistent with heterogeneous firm models predicting that firms' entry/exit decisions reshape network structure before aggregate trade volumes adjust. Second, and most robustly, the documented sector-level heterogeneity offers a structural account of the "distance puzzle": ICT and services sectors exhibit genuine distance compression through network decentralization, while heavy manufacturing maintains geographic constraints through persistent regional modularity. Third, the Granger-causal precedence of network fragility indicators over gravity coefficients establishes an empirical bridge between the production network literature on shock propagation and the gravity framework, with direct relevance for understanding supply chain resilience amid geopolitical fragmentation.

# Introduction {#sec:introduction}

Gravity models serve as the fundamental framework for empirical
international commerce, elucidating the relationship between bilateral
trade and the economic size of countries (usually represented by
\gls{gdp}) as well as trade frictions, particularly geographic distance.
In structural gravity, the income (\`\`mass'') elasticities and distance
elasticity are not simply reduced-form coefficients; they represent
fundamental characteristics and equilibrium entities associated with
bilateral and multilateral trade costs, general equilibrium incidence,
and market accessibility. [@anderson2003; @fally2015; @headmayer2014].
Nevertheless, the majority of practical research regards these
coefficients as invariant within samples or across extensive periods,
despite significant transformations in technology, policy, and global
industrial organisation since the mid-1990s.

A growing literature documents that gravity relationships are not
invariant over time. The so-called distance puzzle—whether distance
matters less in trade—has been debated for decades [@brun2005;
@disdier2008; @berthelon2008; @andersonyotov2010; @novy2013;
@yotov2012]. Although \gls{ict} diffusion and platforms can compress
distance in some contexts [@lendle2016], compositional changes and
quality differentiation can preserve or even amplify the role of
distance in others [@berthelon2008; @hummels2005; @baldwinharrigan2011].
More broadly, time variation in gravity coefficients can reflect
evolving multilateral resistance, changing trade costs (tariff and
non-tariff), supply-chain lengthening or reshoring, or shifts in the
elasticity of substitution [@anderson2003; @headmayer2014; @novy2013;
@eaton2002; @simonovska2014; @egger2015].

At the same time, world trade is a multilayer, evolving network of links
among countries, sectors, and products [@fagiolo2009; @debenedictis2011;
@barigozzi2010; @garlaschelli2004; @cerina2015; @kivela2014]. Network
structure—centrality, clustering, assortativity—both shapes and is
shaped by trade frictions and market size [@chaney2014; @opsahl2010].
The fragmentation of production across borders \glspl{gvc} further
implies that sector- and product-specific gravity relationships may
follow distinct temporal paths as value-added flows rewire the
underlying network [@johnson2012; @koopman2014; @cerina2015;
@antras2013]. Ignoring such heterogeneity risks masking economically and
statistically meaningful dynamics that matter for forecasting,
counterfactual analysis, and policy design.

<!--Treating gravity coefficients as time-invariant can therefore lead to biased inference and misguided policy evaluation. Omitted time variation in multilateral resistance, network interdependence, and sectoral composition can be misattributed to bilateral covariates (e.g., distance), and the prevalence of zero flows and structural breaks compounds these issues [@baldwin2006; @headmayer2014; @fally2015;
@helpman2008; @egger2003; @pesaran2006]. By explicitly modeling and
measuring the time series of gravity coefficients—at the aggregate level
and across sectors and product groups—we can better link trade-cost
changes to network restructuring and identify where and when the law of
gravity bends.-->

The benefits extend beyond fit. Theoretical and empirical research shows that economic networks condition resilience and shock propagation [@acemoglu2012; @carvalho2014; @digiovanni2020; @boehm2019; @bonadio2021; @carvalho2021; @vespignani2012]. If gravity coefficients track the evolving strength of trade frictions and market-access elasticities, their temporal co-movement with network structure can reveal which layers of the trade network (countries, sectors, products) are fragile or robust to shocks, where bottlenecks arise, and how shocks propagate internationally.

The intersection of gravity models and network analysis in international trade research has garnered increasing attention over the past decade, yet remains incompletely explored. Although gravity models have long served as the workhorse for understanding bilateral trade flows based on economic mass and geographic distance [@anderson2003], network science has emerged as a complementary framework for capturing the structural properties and evolutionary dynamics of global trade systems [@sgrignoli2015relation, @serrano2003topology]. @lee2025selfconsistent proposed a data-driven method to infer economic mass directly from trade flows, capturing intrinsic trade capacity as a node-level network attribute; @flori2025carbon introduced a community detection framework based on gravity models to analyse the mesoscale structure of the carbon trade network; @robinson2025electrical derived the gravity model from first principles using an electrical circuit analogy, naturally producing core-periphery structures observed in real trade networks. However, these studies predominantly focus on static or short-term analyses [@he2024symphony; @fang2023global; @jiang2023structural], examining either the application of gravity models to explain network formation or using network indicators as covariates in gravity regressions, without systematically investigating the temporal precedence and Granger-causal relationships between network topology and gravity model parameters using multiple complementary methods.

Critical research gaps remain unaddressed in the literature. First, the mechanism of action—whether network structural changes drive shifts in gravity coefficients or vice versa—has not been subjected to rigorous causality analysis. Although several studies employ \gls{tergm} [@ding2025study; @feng2024patterns] or \gls{qap} [@xing2023structural; @dong2024spatial] to identify determinants of network evolution, these methods primarily test the influence of exogenous factors on network formation rather than the dynamic interplay between endogenous network topology (e.g., fractal dimensions, lacunarity) and gravity model parameters. Second, existing network explorations are incomplete: most studies focus on conventional indicators such as degree centrality,
betweenness, and modularity [@hao2020using; @garcia2016international;
@chen2023complex], while advanced topological measures like local
lacunarity and network box-counting fractal dimensions—which capture
multiscale heterogeneity and self-similarity—remain unexplored in the
gravity model context. Third, research has been fragmented across
specific sectors (e.g., virtual water trade [@xing2023structural], waste
trade [@poon2024industrial], renewable energy [@feng2024patterns]) or
regions, lacking comprehensive studies that examine multiple trade
databases (\gls{oecd} \gls{icio} vs. \gls{cepii}-\gls{baci}) over
extended periods (1995-2022) to assess the robustness and
generalizability of network-gravity relationships. Our research
addresses these \glspl{rg} by

\begin{description}
\item[RG$_1$\label{rg1}] conducting traditional, Bayesian, and \gls{ml}-based panel Granger causality analyses to establish directional temporal relationships between network topology and gravity coefficients,
\item[RG$_2$\label{rg2}] incorporating fractal dimensions and local lacunarity distribution moments (mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis) as novel network indicators that capture multiscale heterogeneity,
\item[RG$_3$\label{rg3}] performing comparative temporal analysis across two major trade databases (\gls{oecd} \gls{icio} and \gls{cepii}-\gls{baci}) spanning 1995--2022, enabling cross-validation at sectoral and product levels,
\item[RG$_4$\label{rg4}] investigating how changes in network structural properties---including modularity, centralization measures, and fractal characteristics---temporally precede or follow shifts in distance sensitivity and \gls{gdp} elasticities.
\end{description}

A comprehensive study examining temporal relationships across different trade networks is essential for several reasons. First, different databases capture distinct dimensions of trade: \gls{oecd} \gls{icio} emphasizes value-added trade and sectoral linkages, while \gls{cepii}-\gls{baci} provides high-resolution product-level bilateral flows. Cross-database validation ensures that observed network-gravity relationships are not artefacts of data construction methodologies but reflect genuine economic phenomena. Second, temporal analysis reveals whether the relationships between network indicators and gravity coefficients are stable or exhibit regime shifts---critical knowledge for building reliable forecasting models. Third, identifying whether network structural properties can serve as leading indicators for changes in distance sensitivity would enable more proactive trade policy design.

<!--A comprehensive study examining temporal relationships across different trade networks is essential for several reasons. First, the global trade landscape has undergone profound structural transformations due to trade liberalization, the rise of global value chains, regional trade agreements, and recent disruptions (2008 financial crisis, \gls{covid}-19 pandemic, geopolitical tensions) [@degroot2020network; @kosowska2020network]. Understanding whether these structural shifts precede or follow changes in fundamental trade determinants (as captured by gravity coefficients) can inform predictions about future trade patterns and policy effectiveness. Second, different databases capture distinct dimensions of trade: \gls{oecd} \gls{icio} emphasizes value-added trade and sectoral linkages, while \gls{cepii}-\gls{baci} provides high-resolution product-level bilateral flows. Cross-database validation ensures that observed network-gravity relationships are not artefacts of data construction methodologies but reflect genuine economic phenomena. Third, temporal analysis reveals whether the relationships between network indicators and gravity coefficients are stable or exhibit regime shifts—critical knowledge for building reliable forecasting models and early warning systems. Finally, from a policy perspective, identifying whether network structural properties (e.g., increasing modularity signaling regionalization, or declining fractal dimension indicating simplification) can serve as leading indicators for changes in distance sensitivity or border effects would enable more proactive trade policy design and multilateral cooperation strategies.-->

We leverage two complementary sources—the \gls{oecd}-\gls{icio}
framework and the \gls{cepii}-\gls{baci} product-level database—to
estimate and analyse time-varying gravity coefficients from 1995 to 2022
at multiple levels of aggregation. This creates a unique opportunity to
relate structural gravity dynamics to network evolution across sectors
and products using consistent, high-quality data [@gaulier2010;
@mayer2011; @timmer2015].

Based on the research gaps we formulated the following \gls{rq}: How do the income and distance coefficients of structural gravity evolve over 1995--2022 at the network-wide, sectoral (\gls{oecd}-\gls{icio}), and product-group (\gls{cepii}-\gls{baci}) levels? Do changes in trade-network structure (centrality, modularity, fractal dimensions, lacunarity) Granger-cause shifts in these gravity coefficients, or vice versa? What patterns of heterogeneity emerge across sectors and products, and what do these dynamics imply for understanding trade network resilience?

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section \ref{background} reviews the relevant literature on structural gravity models, trade networks, time-varying coefficients, and causality methods, identifying the specific gaps our research addresses. Section \ref{material-and-methods} describes the two databases employed (OECD-ICIO and CEPII-BACI), the construction of multiplex trade networks, the network indicators calculated, and the three causality testing methodologies applied. Section \ref{sec:results} presents the empirical findings, including temporal patterns of gravity coefficients, network indicator evolution, correlation analyses, and causality test results across aggregate, sectoral, and product-group levels. Section \ref{sec:discussion} interprets these findings in light of existing theory, discusses the mechanisms connecting network structure to gravity parameters, and examines the heterogeneity across sectors and products. Section \ref{sec:conclusion} summarizes the main contributions, discusses methodological innovations and policy implications, and outlines directions for future research. Technical details on gravity model estimation, network indicator calculations, forecasting methods, and causality testing procedures are provided in the Appendix.

# Theoretical Framework {#sec:theory}

Our analysis is grounded in three interconnected theoretical strands that jointly motivate the hypothesized relationships between trade network topology and gravity model parameters. This framework connects the structural gravity tradition \citep{anderson2003, headmayer2014, yotov2024evolution} with heterogeneous firm trade theory \citep{melitz2015new, chaney2014} and the production network literature \citep{acemoglu2012, baqaee2019macroeconomic}.

## Structural Gravity and the Economics of Distance Elasticity {#subsec:theory_gravity}

The structural gravity model, derived from the seminal contributions of \citet{anderson1979, anderson2003} and extended by \citet{eaton2002}, \citet{helpman2008}, and \citet{melitz2015new}, provides the micro-founded basis for our gravity specifications. In this framework, the distance elasticity $\gamma_t$ is not merely a statistical coefficient but reflects the interaction of bilateral trade costs, the elasticity of substitution between varieties, and---in heterogeneous firm models---the shape of the productivity distribution \citep{carrere2020gravity, arkolakis2012new}.

Two properties of structural gravity are central to our analysis. First, \citet{arkolakis2012new} demonstrated that aggregate welfare gains from trade can be summarized by two sufficient statistics: the domestic expenditure share and the trade elasticity. Since the distance elasticity $\gamma_t$ captures a key component of the trade elasticity, temporal shifts in $\gamma_t$ have direct welfare implications: a declining $|\gamma_t|$ implies increasing gains from trade, while a rising $|\gamma_t|$ signals growing trade frictions with potential welfare losses.

Second, the recent comprehensive surveys by \citet{yotov2024evolution} and \citet{larch2025estimating} establish that structural gravity has evolved from an a-theoretical estimation equation to a full \gls{cge} framework. Our contribution leverages this evolution: by treating year-specific gravity estimates as realizations of a time-varying structural process, we investigate the economic forces---captured by network topology---that drive temporal shifts in these structural parameters.

## Network Topology as Extensive Margin Dynamics {#subsec:theory_networks}

Heterogeneous firm trade models predict that trade liberalization operates through two channels: the \textit{intensive margin} (existing firms trade more) and the \textit{extensive margin} (new firms enter export markets or existing firms exit) \citep{helpman2008, melitz2015new}. \citet{chaney2014} proved theoretically that firm-level heterogeneity in productivity and trade costs endogenously generates network structures with specific topological properties: fat-tailed degree distributions, high clustering, and core-periphery architecture.

We extend these insights by hypothesizing that \textit{changes} in network topology---measured by centrality, modularity, fractal dimension, and lacunarity---primarily reflect extensive margin adjustments: firms entering new markets, forming new trade partnerships, or reorganising supply chains. If these network-level changes are driven by the same trade cost fundamentals that determine gravity coefficients, but adjust at different speeds (because the extensive margin responds faster than the intensive margin), then network topology should exhibit temporal precedence over gravity parameters. This yields three testable hypotheses:

\begin{description}
\item[H$_1$ (Centralization $\rightarrow$ GDP elasticities):] Changes in network centralization and density Granger-cause shifts in GDP elasticities, because new trade links (extensive margin) restructure market access before aggregate flow volumes (intensive margin) fully adjust. Economically, this reflects the ``preferential attachment'' mechanism: as hub economies attract new trade connections, their gravitational pull (GDP elasticity) strengthens with a lag of one year in traditional Granger tests and of four to five years once we require the effect to clear a Random-Forest shadow-feature significance threshold (Appendix \ref{sec:rfgc}).

\item[H$_2$ (Community structure $\rightarrow$ distance elasticity, heterogeneously across sectors):] Changes in network community structure Granger-cause shifts in distance elasticity, because regional trade bloc formation---captured by community structure \citep{caliendo2015estimates}---reduces within-bloc trade frictions with a lag as firms exploit new preferential access. At the aggregate network level this relationship is weak: of our 29 aggregate network indicators, only path-length (\gls{avpl}) and two centrality-adjacent measures Granger-precede the aggregate distance elasticity, and modularity itself does not. We therefore test H$_2$ primarily at the sectoral and product-group level (Figures \ref{fig:causgravsect} and \ref{fig:causgravprod}), where the ``distance puzzle'' \citep{disdier2008} should be attributable to network reorganisation in some, but not all, sectors.

\item[H$_3$ (Network heterogeneity $\rightarrow$ GDP elasticities, and more weakly to distance elasticity):] Multiscale heterogeneity measures (lacunarity, fractal dimension) Granger-cause changes in gravity coefficients, because structural irregularities in trade partner distributions reflect vulnerabilities that propagate through the input-output cascade mechanism \citep{acemoglu2012, baqaee2019macroeconomic}. At the aggregate level this holds clearly for GDP elasticities -- higher lacunarity and lower fractal dimension precede subsequent changes in both origin and destination GDP elasticity -- but not for the aggregate distance elasticity, where none of the four lacunarity moments or fractal dimension pass either the traditional or the Random-Forest shadow-feature test; as with H$_2$, any distance-elasticity effect of network heterogeneity appears to be concentrated in specific sectors and products rather than operating uniformly across the aggregate network (Section \ref{panel-causality-sectoral-and-product-heterogeneity}).
\end{description}

\textbf{Economic Interpretation of Fractal Dimension and Lacunarity.} These two measures are not purely descriptive topological statistics; each maps onto a specific economic mechanism already implicit in the heterogeneous-firm and production-network literatures we build on. Following the network box-counting approach of \citet{songhavlinmakse2005}, the fractal dimension of a trade network summarizes how self-similarly trade linkages are distributed across spatial/relational scales. A lower fractal dimension corresponds to a more hub-and-spoke, hierarchical topology in which a small number of intermediating hub economies account for a disproportionate share of connections at every scale, consistent with \citet{chaney2014}'s prediction that heterogeneous-firm entry generates core-periphery structure; a higher fractal dimension indicates a more space-filling, decentralized pattern of direct bilateral linkages, consistent with a lower effective cost of establishing new bilateral trade relationships (the extensive margin). Lacunarity, in turn, measures the "gappiness" -- the heterogeneity in the size and spacing of gaps between a country's trade partners -- of the network at a given scale (as reflected in our own node-level definition, $\text{LL}_i = \langle r_i^2\rangle/\langle r_i\rangle^2$, Appendix \ref{sec:calcnet}); economically, high lacunarity indicates that a country's trading partners are unevenly distributed in  "network space", concentrated in intensively-connected clusters separated by large gaps to other potential partners. This is precisely the kind of structural irregularity that \citet{baqaee2019macroeconomic} show can amplify the aggregate effect of local shocks nonlinearly, because a shock hitting a densely-connected cluster propagates disproportionately within it before reaching sparsely-connected regions. Rising lacunarity is therefore a leading indicator of increased effective distance sensitivity not because geographic distance itself has changed, but because uneven partner spacing raises the effective (network) distance a shock -- or a new trade relationship -- must travel, a mechanism related to, but distinct from, the geographic distance term already present in the gravity equation. We treat fractal dimension and lacunarity as summarizing multiscale structural heterogeneity that is complementary to, rather than a restatement of, conventional centrality and modularity measures, consistent with the only moderate correlations we document between FDim/LL and degree/eigenvector centrality. In line with H$_3$, the same logic extends this mechanism to the \gls{gdp} elasticities that H$_3$ also predicts: a more space-filling (higher fractal dimension) or more evenly-spaced (lower lacunarity) topology reflects the same extensive-margin process of new bilateral-relationship formation already invoked for centralization under H$_1$, so fractal dimension and lacunarity should Granger-precede changes in both origin- and destination-\gls{gdp} elasticities through this market-access channel, not only the distance elasticity discussed above. Unlike the distance channel, this market-access channel does not imply an unambiguous sign ex ante, so we treat the direction of this relationship for the \gls{gdp} elasticities as an open empirical question, addressed directly by the \gls{gdp} elasticity causality results in Section \ref{sec:results} and revisited in Section \ref{sec:discussion}.

## Production Networks, Shock Propagation, and the Gravity--Resilience Nexus {#subsec:theory_resilience}

The production network literature establishes that microeconomic shocks propagate through input-output linkages and can generate aggregate fluctuations \citep{acemoglu2012, baqaee2019macroeconomic, carvalho2014}. \citet{baqaee2019macroeconomic} demonstrate that this propagation is inherently \textit{nonlinear}: in networks with heterogeneous firms and complementary inputs, small shocks can have disproportionately large aggregate effects. This nonlinearity provides a theoretical basis for our use of Random Forest-based causality testing alongside linear methods.

Direct empirical evidence comes from \citet{boehm2019} (natural disaster propagation) and \citet{bonadio2021} (COVID-19 supply chain transmission). These studies document that network structure---particularly the concentration of trade through hub nodes---determines the speed and magnitude of shock propagation.

Our framework connects this literature to gravity models by proposing that network resilience indicators ---particularly the divergence between random (RRes) and systematic (SRes) attack resilience---capture the structural vulnerability of trade networks to disruptions. When SRes deteriorates relative to RRes, the network becomes increasingly dependent on a few critical hub nodes. Such concentration should, with a lag, affect the effective trade cost structure captured by gravity coefficients, because disruptions to hub countries propagate disproportionately through the network \citep{carvalho2021}. This provides a theoretical mechanism for linking network resilience to gravity coefficient dynamics and connects our analysis to the growing literature on geopolitical fragmentation and supply chain reorganisation \citep{alfaro2023reallocation, freund2024supply}.

# Background


## Structural Gravity Models and Temporal Variation {#subsec:gravity}

The modern structural gravity model provides a theoretical foundation for gravity coefficients and multilateral resistance terms [@anderson1979; @anderson2003; @anderson2011; @headmayer2014; @fally2015]. Advances in estimation address heteroskedasticity and zeros (\gls{ppml}) and advocate high-dimensional fixed effects to capture multilateral resistance and time-varying shocks [@SantosSilvaTenreyro2006; @helpman2008; @santos2011; @headmayer2014; @fally2015]. Against this background, the temporal stability of gravity coefficients has been scrutinized via the distance puzzle and related decompositions [@brun2005; @disdier2008; @berthelon2008; @andersonyotov2010; @yotov2012; @novy2013], with mixed evidence: \gls{ict}-enabled platforms can attenuate distance [@lendle2016], whereas composition and quality can sustain or magnify it [@berthelon2008; @hummels2005; @baldwinharrigan2011]. Micro-founded models of trade costs and elasticities provide additional interpretations for evolving coefficients [@eaton2002; @simonovska2014; @egger2015]. Methodological guidance emphasizes correct specification in panels and the treatment of bilateral dependence [@egger2003; @baldwin2006; @headmayer2014; @pesaran2006; @chudik2015].

Recent surveys by \citet{yotov2024evolution} and \citet{larch2025estimating} have comprehensively documented the evolution of structural gravity from an a-theoretical estimating equation to a full general equilibrium framework. \citet{yotov2024evolution} emphasizes that proper treatment of multilateral resistance terms, zero trade flows, and country-pair heterogeneity is essential for obtaining unbiased gravity estimates. \citet{larch2025estimating} provide specific practical recommendations, including the use of \gls{ppml} estimation \citep{SantosSilvaTenreyro2006} and country-pair fixed effects. Our cross-sectional approach, while departing from the panel fixed-effects standard, is shared with the distance puzzle literature \citep{disdier2008, yotov2012distance} and is necessary for our research design, which requires year-specific coefficient estimates. We address potential biases through \gls{ppml} robustness checks (Appendix \ref{sec:ppml_robust}) and cross-database validation.

\citet{antras2025uncharted} provides a comprehensive overview of the frontier in international trade theory, highlighting the importance of heterogeneous firms, global sourcing, and network effects for understanding modern trade patterns. Our analysis directly addresses his call for empirical work connecting network-level phenomena to structural trade parameters.

## Identification Challenges in Structural Gravity {#subsec:identification}

A critical strand of the gravity literature has focused on identification and estimation challenges that bear directly on the interpretation of time-varying coefficients. We discuss four issues particularly relevant for our analysis, following the comprehensive guides by \citet{headmayer2014}, \citet{yotov2024evolution}, and \citet{larch2025estimating}.

\textit{First, Multilateral Resistance.} \citet{anderson2003} demonstrated that bilateral trade depends not only on bilateral trade costs but also on trade costs with all other partners---the multilateral resistance terms (MRTs). Failing to account for MRTs produces biased and inconsistent estimates of distance and GDP elasticities \citep{headmayer2014, yotov2024evolution}. The standard remedy is exporter- and importer-specific fixed effects, but, as explained in Section \ref{sec:gravity_spec}, these cannot be added to our year-by-year cross-sectional specification \eqref{eq:gravity} without absorbing $\ln(GDP_{i,t})$ or $\ln(GDP_{j,t})$ themselves: within a single year, each exporter (importer) has exactly one GDP value, so the fixed effect and the corresponding GDP elasticity would be perfectly collinear. We instead include nine bilateral controls from the CEPII Gravity database \citep{conte2022cepii} (Section \ref{sec:gravity_spec}), which absorb time-invariant and slow-moving \textit{bilateral} heterogeneity but cannot substitute for genuinely \textit{multilateral} (country-specific, all-partners) resistance terms.

Unlike a specification with exporter-/importer-year fixed effects, our design therefore does not remove within-year multilateral resistance from the dependent variable \textit{by construction}. Our distance and GDP elasticities remain potentially exposed to time-varying MRTs that are correlated with network topology: any Granger-causal link we detect from network topology to the residual gravity coefficients would be \textit{consistent with} network structure proxying for unmodelled MRT dynamics rather than exerting an independent effect, and we cannot rule this out with the current design. We flag this explicitly here and in Section \ref{sec:limitations}, and, for this reason, we describe our findings throughout using temporal-precedence rather than causal language (see our response to the reviewer's first point), and return to this channel in the Discussion (Section \ref{subsec:theory_implications}).

\textit{Second, Endogeneity of Trade Costs.} Trade policy variables (tariffs, FTAs) are potentially endogenous: countries self-select into agreements based on anticipated trade gains \citep{baier2007, larch2025estimating}. Equation \eqref{eq:gravity} includes a joint FTA/WTO-membership indicator among its nine CEPII bilateral controls \citep{conte2022cepii}, together with contiguity, common official and ethnic language, colonial history, common legal origin, and EU membership of either partner (Section \ref{sec:gravity_spec}); several of the omitted-bilateral-factor concerns raised in the distance puzzle literature \citep{disdier2008, brun2005, yotov2012distance} are therefore addressed directly rather than left in the error term. This does not resolve the deeper endogeneity concern that FTA participation is itself a policy choice correlated with unobserved bilateral trade potential, nor does it capture the country-specific policy environments that exporter-/importer-year fixed effects would otherwise absorb (see \textit{First}, above); our distance elasticity should accordingly be interpreted as a partial, not fully causal, effect of geographic distance net of the observed bilateral controls.

\textit{Third, Zero Trade Flows.} The log-linear gravity model drops zero bilateral flows, potentially introducing selection bias \citep{SantosSilvaTenreyro2006, helpman2008}. We address this directly: throughout the paper, Equation \eqref{eq:gravity} is estimated by \gls{ppml} on trade in levels rather than by \gls{ols} on log-transformed trade, which lets zero-flow observations enter the estimation naturally and is robust to heteroskedasticity \citep{SantosSilvaTenreyro2006} (Section \ref{sec:ppml_robust}). Appendix \ref{app:ols_ppml_comparison} reports the corresponding \gls{ols} estimates for comparison and confirms that our \gls{ppml}-based coefficient trajectories are not an artefact of the estimator choice.

\textit{Fourth, the Role of Country-Pair Fixed Effects.} The state-of-the-art in gravity estimation employs country-pair fixed effects in panel settings to absorb all time-invariant bilateral factors, including distance \citep{larch2025estimating, yotov2024evolution}. Our research design deliberately departs from this approach: we \textit{require} cross-sectional distance estimates for each year to construct the time series that are the object of our Granger causality analysis. This design choice is shared with the distance puzzle literature \citep{disdier2008, brun2005, yotov2012distance}, which similarly needs year-specific distance coefficients. \citet{yotov2012distance} demonstrated that the distance puzzle is partly an artefact of omitting domestic trade flows, while our focus is on the \textit{temporal co-movement} between distance coefficients and network topology rather than the absolute level of distance elasticity. We mitigate omitted variable concerns through comprehensive exporter and importer fixed effects in each cross-section and cross-database validation (OECD-ICIO vs. BACI-CEPII).

Because distance itself is time-invariant for a given country pair, this absorption is not merely a stylistic choice but a mechanical identification constraint: a specification with country-pair fixed effects cannot simultaneously deliver an estimate of the distance elasticity, since $\ln Dist_{ij}$ would be perfectly collinear with the pair fixed effect and would be dropped from the regression. Our research question requires precisely the opposite -- a \textit{separate}, identified distance elasticity for every year -- which is why, like the rest of the year-specific distance-puzzle literature \citep{disdier2008, brun2005, yotov2012distance}, we use exporter- and importer-year fixed effects rather than country-pair fixed effects.

## Trade Networks and Multilayer Structure {#subsec:networks}

 The \gls{wtn} exhibits rich, evolving topology---heavy-tailed degree and weight distributions, clustering, and core-periphery features [@fagiolo2009; @garlaschelli2004; @serrano2003]. Recent work has begun to explicitly link gravity model predictions with network topology, demonstrating that network structure both reflects and shapes bilateral trade costs \citep{hood2017gravity}. Network approaches highlight heterogeneity across layers (countries, sectors, products) and the role of centrality for aggregate outcomes [@debenedictis2011; @barigozzi2010; @cerina2015; @kivela2014; @opsahl2010]. Gravity-consistent mechanisms can generate network structure endogenously (e.g., firm-to-firm matching and intermediary roles) [@chaney2014]. The expansion of \glspl{gvc} underscores the need to disaggregate by sector/product and consider value-added flows when connecting gravity to network metrics [@johnson2012; @koopman2014; @antras2013; @cerina2015]. Product-space and related perspectives further link specialization to network proximity [@hidalgo2009].
 
## Heterogeneous Firms and Endogenous Network Formation {#subsec:hetfirms}

A central theoretical insight motivating our analysis comes from the heterogeneous firm trade literature. \citet{melitz2015new} demonstrate that trade liberalization generates welfare gains through a selection channel: the most productive firms enter export markets while the least productive exit. \citet{arkolakis2012new} show that, under certain conditions, aggregate welfare gains can be summarized by two sufficient statistics: the domestic expenditure share and the trade elasticity---precisely the objects our gravity model captures.

Critically, \citet{chaney2014} proved that heterogeneous 
firm models endogenously generate trade network 
structures with specific topological properties. The 
degree distribution, clustering coefficient, and network 
density are all determined by the underlying productivity 
distribution and bilateral trade costs. This implies a 
tight theoretical connection between gravity model 
parameters (reflecting trade costs and elasticities) 
and network topology (reflecting firm entry/exit 
patterns).

\citet{bernard2018networks} survey the growing 
literature on networks and trade, emphasizing that 
firm-level network formation is driven by search 
frictions, relationship-specific investments, and 
information costs distinct from iceberg trade costs. 
This suggests that network topology captures trade 
friction information not fully reflected in distance 
or GDP alone, providing an economic rationale for why 
network indicators add predictive content for gravity 
parameters.

## Time-Varying Gravity Coefficients {#subsec:timevarying}

Several strands explicitly call for or document temporal variation in gravity parameters, particularly the distance elasticity and the incidence of geography [@brun2005; @disdier2008; @berthelon2008; @andersonyotov2010; @yotov2012; @novy2013; @headmayer2014]. These contributions argue that ignoring time variation can confound policy evaluation and mismeasure trade costs, especially when multilateral resistance and compositional effects shift over time. At finer granularity, sector/product heterogeneity motivates estimating and comparing time paths across layers [@baldwinharrigan2011; @hummels2005; @egger2015].

Linking the time paths of gravity coefficients to evolving network structure can identify whether changes in trade frictions or market size elasticities are associated with re-wiring of trade links and re-weighting across sectors/products. This is critical for understanding resilience and international shock transmission—how disruptions in one sector/country propagate through trade linkages [@acemoglu2012; @carvalho2014; @digiovanni2020; @boehm2019; @bonadio2021; @carvalho2021; @vespignani2012]. Despite vast gravity and network literatures, direct causal mapping between time-varying gravity coefficients and structural network metrics remains scarce, especially at product and sector levels with long panels. Our study addresses this gap using consistent estimation on \gls{oecd}-\gls{icio} sectors and \gls{cepii}-\gls{baci} products [@gaulier2010; @mayer2011; @timmer2015].

## Causality Methods for Short Panels {#subsec:methods}

Many sector/product panels feature short time dimensions, necessitating appropriate econometric methods. Classical Granger causality \citep{granger1969} provides the baseline framework; panel extensions \citep{dumitrescu2012} handle cross-sectional units with fixed effects. Bayesian model comparison via Bayes factors \citep{kass1995} offers an alternative that naturally incorporates parameter uncertainty and avoids multiple testing issues. Complementing linear methods with \gls{ml}-based approaches such as Random Forests \citep{breiman2001} can capture nonlinear relationships that traditional tests may miss. Because time-series dependence invalidates naive cross-validation, blocked or rolling procedures are needed for predictive evaluation \citep{bergmeir2018}.

Because time-series dependence invalidates naive random folds, blocked/rolling cross-validation and predictive evaluation are needed to guard against overfitting and to compare methods fairly [@arlot2010; @bergmeir2012; @bergmeir2018; @varian2014; @athey2017].-->

## Network Resilience and Shock Propagation {#subsec:resilience}

Production and trade networks amplify or dampen shocks depending on topology and link weights [@acemoglu2012; @carvalho2014; @vespignani2012]. Firm- and sector-level evidence shows how input linkages transmit shocks within and across borders [@boehm2019; @digiovanni2020; @carvalho2021; @bonadio2021]. By relating time variation in gravity coefficients to changes in network metrics, one can identify when higher distance sensitivity or lower market-size elasticity coincides with more brittle structures (e.g., hub-dependence, low redundancy), informing policy about diversification, regionalization, or supply-chain risk. To our knowledge, few studies jointly model the dynamics of structural gravity coefficients and the co-evolution of sector/product-level network structure; doing so can bridge the structural gravity and production-network literatures.

The empirical literature on the intersection of gravity models and
network analysis in trade has expanded considerably since the mid-2010s,
driven by advances in computational methods and data availability. Early
contributions focused primarily on applying gravity models to predict
trade flows, treating network structure as an exogenous outcome rather
than an interactive system component. More recent work has begun to
recognize the bidirectional relationship between network topology and
trade determinants, employing sophisticated statistical frameworks such as \gls{ergm}, Temporal \gls{ergm} (\gls{tergm}), and \gls{qap} to disentangle the complex interplay between structural and behavioural factors. However, as detailed in Table \ref{tab:literature_review}, the existing body of research exhibits important limitations: most studies are sector-specific or geographically constrained, few employ explicit causality testing beyond correlation analysis, and almost none investigate advanced topological indicators such as fractal dimensions or lacunarity. <!--This review synthesizes findings from recent studies to contextualize our research contributions. -->

\addlinespace

\cite{chung2020spatial} & Meat trade (134 countries) & 1995–2015 & Structural changes, consolidated networks & Partial (meat) & Dynamic & Yes & Combined network modeling with cluster analysis to track structural changes in global meat trade over two decades. In consolidated networks, the presence of trade agreements and shorter geographic distances are strongly associated with increased bilateral meat trade volumes. \\
\addlinespace

\cite{dong2024spatial} & 282 Chinese cities & 2006–2019 & Core-edge, community, microstructure, centrality & Partial (logistics carbon, China) & Dynamic & Yes (\gls{ergm} + \gls{qap}) & Applied modified gravity models and \gls{ergm} to analyse spatial correlation patterns in logistics carbon emission efficiency across Chinese cities. Financial investment, government concern, international openness, population density, and innovation ability all facilitate spatial correlation formation in the network.  \\
\addlinespace

\cite{chen2023complex} & photovoltaic trade (bilateral) & 2000–2019 & Small-world, disassortativity, reciprocity, transitivity, stability & Partial (photovoltaic) & Dynamic & Yes (\gls{ergm}) & Photovoltaic trade networks exhibit small-world, disassortative, and low reciprocity characteristics. Network formation is driven by transitivity, reciprocity, and stability, combined with gravity factors including WTO membership, continental proximity, asymmetrical development levels, and regional trade agreements.  \\
\addlinespace

\cite{duenas2023structure} & Music videos (GDELT implied) & N/S & Topology, modularity, asymmetric links, diffusion channels & Partial (cultural diffusion) & N/S & Yes & Applied gravity models to identify factors shaping global music diffusion networks. Found that cultural, geographic, and historical factors are primary drivers of network formation, while economic factors play a surprisingly minor role in cultural trade patterns. \\
\addlinespace

\cite{ryczkowski2017transfer} & Air transport & N/S & Hidden subflows, distance coeff. & Partial (air transport) & N/S & Yes & Developed a model for transfer flights that exploits discrepancies in standard gravity models to discover hidden subflows in the global passenger air-transport network. Successfully retrieved the gravity distance coefficient and suggested its correspondence to network fractal dimension. \\

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\end{landscape}

The synthesis of this literature reveals several key patterns. Most studies focus on partial trade networks examining specific sectors or products, with few analysing complete global networks over extended periods. While the field has evolved toward dynamic analysis using \gls{ergm}/\gls{tergm} frameworks and \gls{qap} models, true causal inference techniques---such as Granger causality tests---are conspicuously absent. The literature exhibits substantial overlap in basic indicators (degree centrality, betweenness, modularity) but lacks exploration of advanced topological measures like fractal dimensions or lacunarity, despite theoretical arguments that multiscale structural properties may fundamentally relate to gravity model parameters.

notably, no study in our review simultaneously analyses both \gls{oecd}
\gls{icio} and \gls{cepii}-\gls{baci} to compare value-added vs.
gross trade perspectives. \textbf{Static vs. dynamic approaches:} The
field has clearly evolved toward dynamic analysis, with most studies
explicitly modeling temporal evolution or changes over multiple time
periods. Methodological sophistication has increased correspondingly,
with \gls{ergm}/\gls{tergm} frameworks and \gls{qap} models becoming
standard tools for distinguishing endogenous network effects from
exogenous covariates. While all studies claim to conduct "causality"
analysis, most employ correlation-based methods (\gls{qap}) or

than establish directional causation. True causal inference
techniques—such as Granger causality tests, instrumental variables, or
convergent cross-mapping—are conspicuously absent. The literature
exhibits substantial overlap in basic indicators (degree centrality,
betweenness, core-periphery structure, small-world properties) but lacks
exploration of advanced topological measures. No study examines local
lacunarity, network box-counting fractal dimensions, or the distribution
moments (mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis) of node-level heterogeneity

In comparison, our research advances the field in four critical dimensions. \textit{First}, we conduct genuine temporal causality analysis using traditional, Bayesian and \gls{ml}-based Granger causality tests and related methods to establish whether network indicators lead, lag, or co-evolve with gravity coefficients (see \nameref{c1}). \textit{Second}, we introduce novel network indicators—fractal dimensions and local lacunarity distributions—that capture scale-free properties and spatial heterogeneity more comprehensively than conventional metrics (see \nameref{c2}). \textit{Third}, we perform parallel analyses on two major trade databases (OECD ICIO and BACI-CEPII) spanning 1995–2022, enabling robust cross-validation and comparison of value-added vs. product-level trade patterns (see \nameref{c1}). \textit{Fourth}, we examine complete trade networks rather than sector-specific slices, providing a system-level perspective on how macrostructural changes relate to fundamental trade determinants (see \nameref{c3}). These innovations position our study as the first comprehensive, methodologically rigorous investigation of bidirectional temporal relationships between network topology and gravity model parameters, addressing the critical gaps identified in the existing literature.

\begin{description}
\item[C$_1$ \label{c1}]  (Theoretical): We provide systematic evidence of temporal precedence -- not structural causal identification -- linking the \textit{extensive margin} of trade (network topology formation) to the \textit{intensive margin} (gravity coefficient magnitudes), bridging two previously disconnected literatures: the structural gravity framework \citep{anderson2003, headmayer2014, yotov2024evolution} and the production network approach \citep{acemoglu2012, chaney2014, bernard2018networks}. Our finding that network topology changes Granger-precede gravity shifts---but rarely vice versa---is consistent with heterogeneous firm models \citep{helpman2008, melitz2015new} predicting that firm-level entry/exit decisions (reflected in topology) temporally precede aggregate trade pattern adjustments (reflected in gravity): as discussed in Section \ref{sec:limitations}, common shocks to both series cannot be ruled out, so we treat this as suggestive rather than definitive support for the mechanism.

\item[C$_2$ \label{c2}] (Empirical): We document that the ``distance puzzle'' \citep{disdier2008} is not a unitary phenomenon but a composite of heterogeneous, sector-specific dynamics: services and ICT sectors exhibit declining distance sensitivity consistent with digital trade theories \citep{lendle2016, antras2025uncharted}, while heavy manufacturing maintains stable geographic constraints aligned with transport cost models \citep{hummels2005}. This heterogeneity has first-order implications for understanding global value chain resilience \citep{bonadio2021, carvalho2021} and the differential impact of geopolitical fragmentation across sectors \citep{alfaro2023reallocation, freund2024supply}.

\item[C$_3$ (Methodological--Policy):] \label{c3} We introduce a triangulated causality framework combining traditional, Bayesian, and machine learning approaches with novel network indicators (fractal dimensions, lacunarity moments) to establish that network topology serves as a 1--4 year leading indicator for gravity coefficient shifts. This provides actionable early warning capacity for policymakers monitoring trade friction evolution and supply chain vulnerability.
\end{description}

These contributions directly address the identified research gaps: \nameref{c1} responds to \nameref{rg3} and \nameref{rg4} by providing comprehensive temporal analysis across databases; \nameref{c2} addresses \nameref{rg1} and \nameref{rg2} through rigorous causality testing with novel indicators; and \nameref{c3} tackles \nameref{rg4} by documenting systematic heterogeneity patterns.

## Databases Used and Developed {#sec:data}

This section describes the two primary data sources used in our analysis
and the construction of edge lists for multiplex network analysis. This
corresponds to \textbf{Step 1 (Data Collection and Preparation)} and
\textbf{Step 2 (Multiplex Network Construction)} of our research
framework.

### OECD Inter-Country Input-Output Database (OECD-ICIO) {#subsec:oecd_icio}

The OECD Inter-Country Input-Output (ICIO) database provides a
comprehensive framework for analysing global value chains and
inter-sectoral linkages across countries. From this database, we
exclusively utilize the \textbf{transaction matrix $\mathbf{Z}$}, which
captures intermediate consumption flows between country-sector pairs.

The transaction matrix $\mathbf{Z}$ is organised as a block matrix where
each element $z_{ij}^{rs}$ represents the value of intermediate goods
and services flowing from sector $r$ in country $i$ to sector $s$ in
country $j$. The database covers: (1) *Time period:* 1995--2020 (annual
data); (2) *Countries:* 76 economies (OECD members and major non-OECD
economies); (3) *Sectors:* 45 industries based on \gls{isic} Rev. 4
classification.

From the transaction matrix $\mathbf{Z}$, we construct a directed,
weighted multiplex network where: (1) *nodes* represent countries; (2)
*layers* represent economic sectors; (3) *edges* capture trade flows
between countries, differentiated by *origin* and *destination* sectors;
(4) *inter-layer connections* are explicitly modelled, representing
cross-sectoral value chain linkages.

The edge list structure is defined in Table \ref{tab:oecd_edgelist}:

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Edge list structure for OECD-ICIO multiplex network}
\label{tab:oecd_edgelist}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lp{9cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\texttt{Year} & Reference year $t \in \{1995, 1996, \ldots, 2022\}$ \\
\texttt{Node$_i$} & Origin country (ISO 3-letter code) \\
\texttt{Layer$_i$} & Origin sector (\gls{isic} Rev. 4 code) \\
\texttt{Node$_j$} & Destination country (ISO 3-letter code) \\
\texttt{Layer$_j$} & Destination sector (\gls{isic} Rev. 4 code) \\
\texttt{Volume} & Transaction value in millions USD \\
\texttt{Quantity} & Physical quantity (where available) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Since quantities are not always interpretable, we worked with volume in
all cases. The list of sectors is detailed in Table \ref{tab:industries}

The following example presents an edge list format:

\begin{center}
2019 | DEU | C29 | USA | C30 | 4,523.7 | --
\end{center}

In this example Germany's motor vehicle sector (C29) exports \$4,523.7
million worth of intermediate goods to the US transport equipment sector
(C30) in 2019.

The presence of different origin and destination layers
(\texttt{Layer$_i$} $\neq$ \texttt{Layer$_j$}) explicitly captures
inter-layer connections, which is a distinguishing feature of the
OECD-ICIO multiplex network.

### BACI-CEPII International Trade Database {#subsec:cepii_baci}

The \gls{baci} database, maintained by \gls{cepii}, provides harmonized
bilateral trade flows at the product level using the \gls{hs}
classification. The list of product groups is listed in Table
\ref{tab:BACIPROD}.

The BACI database contains: (1) *time period:* 1995--2022 (annual data);
(2) *countries:* Over 200 reporting economies. (3) *products:* 6-digit
HS codes (approximately 5,000 product categories); (4) *volume:* trade
values (thousands USD) and (5) *quantities:* in metric tons.

We construct three distinct multiplex networks based on different
product aggregation levels:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Product Group Level (HS-2):} First two characters of HS code (approximately 97 product groups)
    \item \textbf{Product Subgroup Level (HS-4):} First four characters of HS code (approximately 1,200 subgroups)
    \item \textbf{Product Level (HS-6):} Full six-digit HS code (approximately 5,000 products)
\end{enumerate}

For the  BACI-CEPII networks: (1) *nodes* represent countries; (2)
*layers* represent products (at the chosen aggregation level); (3)
*edges* capture bilateral trade flows.

*Inter-layer connections* are not defined, as products are treated as
independent layers without explicit cross-product linkages.

The edge list structure is is provided in \ref{tab:baci_edgelist}:

\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Description} \\
\midrule
\texttt{Year} & Reference year $t \in \{1995, 1996, \ldots, 2022\}$ \\
\texttt{Product$_k$} & Product identifier (HS-2, HS-4, or HS-6 code) \\
\texttt{Node$_i$} & Origin (exporting) country \\
\texttt{Node$_j$} & Destination (importing) country \\

### Constructed Analytical Databases {#sec:constructed_databases}

\label{sec:gravity_spec}

This section describes the analytical databases constructed from the multiplex networks, integrating network metrics with gravity model coefficients. This corresponds to
\textbf{Step 3 (Network Metrics Calculation)},
\textbf{Step 4 (Gravity Model Estimation)}, and
\textbf{Step 6 (Correlation and Causality Analysis)} of our research
framework.

For each year $t$, product $k$ (or sector $s$), we estimate the
following gravity model:

\begin{equation}
Trade_{ij,t}^{k} = \exp\left(\alpha + \beta_{o,t}^{k} \ln(GDP_{i,t}) + \beta_{d,t}^{k} \ln(GDP_{j,t}) + \gamma_t^{k} \ln(Distance_{ij}) + \sum_{m=1}^{9} \delta_{m,t}^{k} D_{m,ij}\right) \varepsilon_{ij,t}
\label{eq:gravity}
\end{equation}

\noindent We now estimate \eqref{eq:gravity} by \gls{ppml} \citep{SantosSilvaTenreyro2006} rather than by log-linearized \gls{ols}: the dependent variable is trade in levels (not logged), which allows zero trade flows to enter the estimation without ad hoc adjustment, while the continuous regressors (distance and the two GDP terms) remain log-transformed so that $\beta_{o,t}^{k}$, $\beta_{d,t}^{k}$, and $\gamma_t^{k}$ retain their interpretation as elasticities and stay directly comparable to the \gls{ols} estimates we report as a robustness check (Appendix \ref{app:ols_ppml_comparison}). The term $\sum_{m=1}^{9} \delta_{m,t}^{k} D_{m,ij}$ adds nine time-invariant and time-varying bilateral control variables from the CEPII Gravity database \citep{conte2022cepii}: common official language ($D_1$, \texttt{comlang\_off}), common ethnic language ($D_2$, \texttt{comlang\_ethno}), contiguity ($D_3$, \texttt{contig}), a colonial relationship post-1945 ($D_4$, \texttt{col45}), an ever-colonial relationship ($D_5$, \texttt{col\_dep\_ever}), a common legal origin pre-transition ($D_6$, \texttt{comleg\_pretrans}), joint free-trade-agreement/WTO membership ($D_7$, \texttt{fta\_wto}), and EU membership of the origin ($D_8$, \texttt{eu\_o}) and destination ($D_9$, \texttt{eu\_d}) country. As we discuss in Section \ref{sec:limitations}, standard country-pair or exporter/importer fixed effects cannot be added to \eqref{eq:gravity} without changing our year-by-year cross-sectional design: with one observation per pair per year, a pair fixed effect would saturate the data, and an exporter- or importer-level fixed effect would be collinear with, and would absorb, $\ln(GDP_{i,t})$ or $\ln(GDP_{j,t})$ -- precisely the elasticities this study estimates. The nine CEPII covariates are therefore the most disaggregated bilateral controls that can be added without sacrificing identification of $\beta_{o,t}^{k}$, $\beta_{d,t}^{k}$, and $\gamma_t^{k}$.

\noindent The estimated coefficients that serve as dependent variables in the subsequent network analysis ($Y$) remain unchanged from the original design:

\begin{itemize}
    \item $\beta_{o,t}^{k}$: Origin (exporter) GDP elasticity for product/sector $k$ in year $t$
    \item $\beta_{d,t}^{k}$: Destination (importer) GDP elasticity for product/sector $k$ in year $t$
    \item $\gamma_t^{k}$: Distance elasticity (distance dependence) for product/sector $k$ in year $t$
\end{itemize}

\noindent The nine $\delta_{m,t}^{k}$ coefficients are estimated jointly with $\beta_{o,t}^{k}$, $\beta_{d,t}^{k}$, and $\gamma_t^{k}$ in every cross-section, but -- consistent with our focus on distance and market-size elasticities -- are not themselves carried forward as $Y$ variables into the network-causality analysis; we report their sign stability across years in Appendix \ref{app:ols_ppml_comparison} instead of reproducing 9 additional coefficient panels in the main text.

Network-level and node-level indicators ($X$) computed for each year.
Applied network-level indicators are listed in the Appendix in Table
\ref{tab:networklevelind} and node-level indicators are listed in Table
\ref{tab:nodelevelind}. The two-dimensional panel database aggregates network-level metrics across all layers, providing a time-series perspective on global trade network evolution.

The two-dimensional panel database aggregates network-level metrics 
across all layers. Each row represents a year, with columns containing 
gravitational coefficients ($\beta_{o,t}$, $\beta_{d,t}$, $\gamma_t$) 
and network indicators (Density, Modularity, etc.). An example entry:

\begin{center}
\texttt{1995 | 0.842 | 0.756 | $-$1.234 | 0.432 | 0.567 | \ldots}
\end{center}

\noindent where the values represent Year, $\beta_{o,t}$, $\beta_{d,t}$, 
$\gamma_t$, Density$_t$, and Modularity$_t$ respectively.

Three-dimensional databases maintain product/sector disaggregation,
enabling analysis of heterogeneity across trade categories. For the 
BACI-CEPII product-level database, each row represents a year-product 
combination with gravitational coefficients and node-level indicators:

\begin{center}
\texttt{1995 | 87 | 0.912 | 0.845 | $-$1.456 | 45.2 | 0.234 | \ldots}
\end{center}

\noindent representing Year, Product (HS-2 code), $\beta_{o,t}^{k}$, 
$\beta_{d,t}^{k}$, $\gamma_t^{k}$, Degree Centrality, and Betweenness 
Centrality respectively.

Similarly, for the OECD-ICIO sector-level database:

\begin{center}
\texttt{1995 | C29 | 0.876 | 0.812 | $-$1.534 | 38.4 | 42.1 | \ldots}
\end{center}

\noindent representing Year, Sector (\gls{isic} code), $\beta_{o,t}^{s}$, 
$\beta_{d,t}^{s}$, $\gamma_t^{s}$, In-Degree Centrality, and Out-Degree 
Centrality respectively.

Following \textbf{Step 6 (Correlation and Causality Analysis)}, we
construct result matrices that capture the relationship between
gravitational coefficients and network structural parameters across
different time lags.

For each gravitational coefficient (distance, origin GDP, destination
GDP), we create a two-dimensional matrix where *rows* represents network
indicators (node-level and network-level metrics); *columns* represents
sectors (OECD-ICIO) or product groups (BACI-CEPII) and *cell values*
represents the optimal lag length (1--5 years) from Granger causality
tests or a correlation value in a correlation analysis.

## Employed Network and Gravity Indicators {#sec:indicators}

<!--This section provides a consolidated overview of the indicators used throughout the empirical analysis. This section provides a consolidated overview of the indicators used throughout the empirical analysis, organised into dependent variables (gravity coefficients) and independent variables (network metrics). The indicator selection directly addresses \ref{rg2} by incorporating not only conventional network measures (centrality, modularity, clustering) but also novel topological indicators---specifically, fractal dimensions and the four moments of local lacunarity distributions (mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis)---that capture multiscale heterogeneity in trade network structure.

### Employed Network and Gravity Indicators 

Following \textbf{Step 4} of the research framework (Figure \ref{fig:material}), we estimate time-varying gravity coefficients for each year, sector, and product group. Table \ref{tab:gravity_coefficients} summarizes these dependent variables.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Gravity model coefficients (dependent variables $Y$)}
\label{tab:gravity_coefficients}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llp{7cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Symbol} & \textbf{Name} & \textbf{Interpretation} \\
\midrule
$\gamma_t^{(k)}$ & Distance coefficient & Elasticity of trade with respect to geographic distance; captures trade friction intensity \\
$\beta_{o,t}^{(k)}$ & Origin (exporter) GDP coefficient & Elasticity with respect to exporter economic mass; reflects supply-side capacity \\
$\beta_{d,t}^{(k)}$ & Destination (importer) GDP coefficient & Elasticity with respect to importer economic mass; reflects demand-side market access \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The calculations of gravity coefficients are provided in Appendix \ref{sec:calcgrav}.

Network indicators are computed following \textbf{Step 3} of the research framework. We employ both network-level metrics (characterising the entire trade network) and node-level metrics (computed for individual countries and subsequently aggregated). Table \ref{tab:indicator_groups} organises these indicators by the trade network phenomena they capture, while Table \ref{tab:indicator_gravity_link} explicates their theoretical connections to gravity model coefficients.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Network indicators grouped by trade network phenomena}
\label{tab:indicator_groups}
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{2.8cm}p{4.5cm}p{7cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Phenomenon} & \textbf{Indicators} & \textbf{Interpretation of Temporal Changes} \\
\midrule

\textit{Market Concentration \& Dominance} & 
\gls{dzi}, \gls{dzo}, \gls{bz}, \gls{prz}, \gls{hz}, \gls{pz}; and mean values of \gls{bc}, \gls{ec}, and \gls{prc} & 
Increasing centralization indicates growing dominance of hub economies in trade intermediation. Rising values signal higher systemic risk from hub dependence; declining values suggest more distributed, polycentric trade patterns. \\
\addlinespace

\textit{Trade Intensity \& Connectivity} & 
\gls{dens}, \gls{avpl}, \gls{gle}, \gls{ale}; and mean values of \gls{dci}, \gls{dco}, \gls{sci}, and \gls{sco} & 
Rising density and efficiency indicate deepening trade integration and reduced effective distance between economies. Increasing average path length signals fragmentation or emergence of barriers; declining connectivity reflects trade disintegration or regionalization. \\
\addlinespace

\textit{Clustering \& Regionalization} & 
\gls{trans}, \gls{mod}, \gls{assort} & 
Increasing modularity and transitivity indicate formation of regional trade blocs and preferential trading clusters. Rising assortativity suggests large economies increasingly trade with each other (rich-club formation); changes reflect shifting balance between globalization and regionalization. \\
\addlinespace

\textit{Hierarchical Structure \& Complexity} & 
\gls{fdim}, 1-4 moments of \gls{ll} (LL\_m1, LL\_m2, LL\_m3, LL\_m4) & 
Fractal dimension captures self-similarity across scales; higher values indicate more complex, space-filling network structure. Lacunarity moments measure heterogeneity in trade partner distributions. Temporal changes signal structural phase transitions in network organisation. \\
\addlinespace

\textit{Network Resilience \& Vulnerability} & 
\acrshort{rres}, \acrshort{sres} & 
\acrlong{rres} vs. \acrlong{sres} reveals vulnerability to different disruption types. Declining resilience indicates increasing fragility; divergence between \acrshort{rres} and \acrshort{sres} signals hub-dependent structure vulnerable to targeted shocks. \\
\addlinespace

\textit{Local Trade Patterns} & 
\gls{mot}, Trace; mean values of \gls{hc}, \gls{ac}, \gls{kc}, and \gls{kcr} & 
Motif frequencies capture recurring local configurations (mutual, chain, cyclic patterns). Hub and authority centralities reveal directional influence in value chains. Changes indicate evolving micro-structure of trade relationships and value chain positioning. \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
