## Theoretical Implications: From Network Topology to Trade Theory {#subsec:theory_implications}

Our Granger causality results have three principal theoretical implications that advance international trade theory beyond the methodological contributions.

### Extensive Margin Dynamics: Temporal-Precedence Evidence from Macro {#extensive-margin-dynamics-causal-evidence-from-macro-data}

The finding that network topology changes temporally precede gravity coefficient shifts by 1--4 years (confirming H$_1$ and H$_2$) provides systematic dynamic, macro-level evidence of temporal precedence consistent with the extensive margin mechanism proposed by heterogeneous firm models \citep{helpman2008, melitz2015new, chaney2014}; as with our other causal-sounding claims, we describe this as Granger-style predictive evidence rather than structural causal proof (Section \ref{sec:limitations}). While micro-level studies have documented the importance of extensive vs. intensive margins in static decompositions \citep{helpman2008}, the \textit{temporal ordering} at the network level has not been established. Our results show that when trade costs change (due to technology, policy, or global shocks), the network topology adjusts first (reflecting firm entry/exit---the extensive margin), and only subsequently do aggregate gravity coefficients shift (reflecting volume adjustments---the intensive margin). The 1--4 year lag is economically meaningful: it reflects the time needed for firms' export market entry decisions to translate into measurable changes in aggregate bilateral trade patterns.

### A Structural Account of Sectoral Heterogeneity in the Distance Puzzle {#a-structural-resolution-of-the-distance-puzzle}

Our sector-level analysis offers a novel, structural resolution to the long-debated distance puzzle \citep{disdier2008, brun2005, yotov2012distance}. The aggregate decline in distance elasticity masks two countervailing forces:

\begin{enumerate}
\item A \textit{genuine} reduction in distance sensitivity for digitally tradable services and ICT products (NDA$_1$ cluster), driven by technology-enabled trade cost reduction \citep{lendle2016}. These sectors exhibit rapidly declining modularity---trade links become geographically dispersed as digital technologies reduce the cost of serving distant markets.

\item \textit{Persistent} distance sensitivity for physically intensive goods (NDA$_3$ cluster), consistent with \citet{hummels2005}'s finding that transport costs for bulky goods have not declined proportionally. These sectors maintain high modularity---regional trade concentration persists because transport costs remain the binding constraint.
\end{enumerate}

The network topology provides the \textit{mechanism}: the Granger-causal link from modularity to distance elasticity (H$_2$) shows that the distance puzzle is fundamentally a \textit{composition effect} operating through network reorganisation. As the global trade network's composition shifts toward services (declining modularity, declining distance sensitivity), the aggregate distance elasticity falls---but this masks the persistent role of distance in goods trade. This resolution bridges the contradictory findings in the literature: \citet{disdier2008}'s observation that distance remains important in meta-analysis is consistent with our goods-sector results, while \citet{lendle2016}'s finding of declining distance effects applies specifically to our services/ICT clusters.

### Network Fragility and the Geography of Trade Costs

A novel theoretical insight emerges from the confirmation of H3: the strong causal relationship between lacunarity moments and gravity coefficients. Lacunarity captures the ``gappiness'' of the trade partner distribution across geographic scales. When lacunarity increases---trade becomes more spatially heterogeneous---our results show that distance sensitivity subsequently rises. This is consistent with \citet{baqaee2019macroeconomic}'s nonlinear amplification mechanism: as trade networks become more uneven in their geographic distribution, disruptions to concentrated hubs propagate disproportionately, effectively increasing the gravity of distance in trade.

This finding connects the gravity framework to the production network literature in a way not previously documented, and has direct implications for the ongoing debate about geopolitical fragmentation \citep{alfaro2023reallocation, freund2024supply}. The documented 1--4 year lag between network restructuring and gravity coefficient adjustment implies that the effects of recent reshoring and friendshoring initiatives on measured trade frictions may not be fully visible in gravity estimates for several years. Policymakers relying on current gravity estimates may therefore underestimate the eventual impact of supply chain reorganisation policies. Our framework provides a tool for \textit{nowcasting} these effects using network topology as a leading indicator. This distance-side finding is not the whole picture, however: the Random Forest results (Figure \ref{fig:rfnetcaus}(b)--(c)) show that the local lacunarity moments (LL\_m1 through LL\_m4) and fractal dimension (FDim) are also among the more important predictors of both origin- and destination-\gls{gdp} elasticities, consistent with the market-access channel outlined in Section \ref{sec:theory}. Because neither the Granger tests nor Random Forest importance scores identify the sign of this relationship, we treat whether structural heterogeneity ultimately strengthens or dampens the \gls{gdp} elasticities as an open question for future research rather than infer a direction from significance alone.


## Relating Findings to Previous Research {#subsec:literature_connection}

Our results both confirm and extend previous findings in the gravity and network trade literature.

The declining aggregate distance elasticity confirms the pattern documented by \citet{brun2005} and \citet{disdier2008}, while our disaggregated analysis extends their work by showing that this aggregate trend conceals substantial sectoral heterogeneity---some sectors show increasing distance sensitivity even as others decline. This reconciles apparently contradictory findings in the literature \citep{berthelon2008, yotov2012} by showing that different sample compositions can yield different aggregate patterns.

Our finding that network centralization strongly correlates with \gls{gdp} elasticity extends \citet{fagiolo2009}'s observation that network centrality affects trade outcomes, demonstrating that this relationship operates not just cross-sectionally but through time and exhibits causal structure. The temporal precedence of network changes over gravity coefficient changes is a novel finding that suggests network analysis can provide leading indicators for shifts in fundamental trade parameters.

The identification of fractal dimension and lacunarity as predictors of gravity coefficients represents a genuinely new contribution. While \citet{garcia2016international} connected fractal properties to trade network structure, we demonstrate that these measures have predictive content for the evolution of gravity parameters---a finding with both theoretical significance (suggesting scale-free properties matter for trade costs) and practical applications (providing early warning indicators for structural change).

The systematic heterogeneity in network-gravity relationships across sectors extends the product-level gravity literature \citep{baldwinharrigan2011, hummels2005} by showing that not only do gravity coefficients differ across products, but so do the relationships between these coefficients and network structure. This finding suggests that one-size-fits-all approaches to modeling trade networks may miss important category-specific dynamics.

Our findings also speak to several recent developments in the trade literature. \citet{antras2025uncharted} identifies the interaction between global sourcing decisions and network effects as one of the ``uncharted waters'' of international trade theory. Our documentation of Granger-causal relationships between network topology and gravity parameters provides empirical evidence for exactly this interaction, showing that the network structure of global sourcing (captured by our multiplex trade networks) has measurable, temporally leading effects on the fundamental trade parameters. Similarly, \citet{freund2024supply} document that US trade policy is already reshaping global supply chains; our framework provides a tool for monitoring how such policy-driven network restructuring will eventually manifest in measured trade frictions.

The growing literature on geopolitical fragmentation and ``friendshoring'' \citep{alfaro2023reallocation} raises the question of whether the decades-long decline in aggregate distance sensitivity will reverse. Our modularity-based analysis (H2) suggests that if trade network modularity increases---as friendshoring policies would imply---aggregate distance sensitivity should subsequently rise. The forecast trajectories in our analysis, which project continued but decelerating decline in $|\gamma_t|$ through 2030, may therefore underestimate future distance sensitivity if current geopolitical trends intensify.


# Conclusion {#sec:conclusion}

<!--This study has investigated the temporal co-evolution of structural gravity coefficients and trade network topology using two complementary databases spanning 1995--2022. By analysing distance and \gls{gdp} elasticities at aggregate, sectoral, and product-group levels, and relating their dynamics to a comprehensive set of network indicators, we have addressed the question of whether---and in what sense---the world is getting smaller in terms of trade frictions.

Our analysis yields several principal findings. First, aggregate distance elasticity has declined moderately over the observation period, but this trend masks substantial heterogeneity: service sectors show pronounced declines while heavy manufacturing maintains stable distance sensitivity. Second, network structure and gravity coefficients exhibit strong contemporaneous correlations, with centralization measures correlating at $|r| > 0.9$ with mass elasticities. Third, and most importantly, Granger causality tests reveal that network structural changes---particularly in modularity, centralization, and lacunarity---temporally precede shifts in gravity coefficients, suggesting that network analysis can provide leading indicators for changes in fundamental trade parameters.

## Methodological Contributions {#subsec:method_contributions}

This study advances the methodology for analysing network-gravity relationships in four dimensions.

\textit{First, methodological triangulation.} We demonstrate that employing three complementary causality testing approaches---traditional panel Granger tests, Bayesian model comparison, and Random Forest-based importance analysis---yields more robust and nuanced findings than any single method. The approximately 70\% convergence rate across methods for core findings, combined with method-specific insights (particularly RF-detected nonlinearities), provides a template for future trade network studies.

\textit{Second, novel network indicators.} We introduce fractal dimensions and the four moments of local lacunarity distributions to the trade network literature. These indicators capture multiscale heterogeneity missed by conventional measures and demonstrate significant predictive content for gravity parameter evolution, with LL\_m2 and LL\_m3 emerging among the top five predictors across all specifications.

\textit{Third, cross-database validation.} The parallel analysis of OECD-ICIO (value-added, sectoral) and CEPII-BACI (gross flows, product-level) databases demonstrates that network-gravity relationships are robust to alternative trade conceptualizations. This addresses a critical gap in the literature, where single-database studies cannot distinguish genuine patterns from data construction artefacts.

\textit{Fourth, temporal clustering integration.} The application of Generalized Network-based Dimensionality Analysis (GNDA) to identify temporal clusters of sectors and products provides a principled approach to handling the heterogeneity that aggregate analyses typically mask. The consistent emergence of 2--4 clusters across all aggregation levels suggests natural groupings in trade friction dynamics that future research and policy can exploit.

## Practical Applications}\label{subsec:practical

The findings of this study have several practical applications for trade analysts, forecasters, and policymakers.

\textit{For trade forecasting:} The documented temporal precedence of network indicators over gravity coefficients suggests a practical forecasting strategy. Analysts can monitor network topology measures---particularly modularity, centralization indices, and lacunarity---as early warning indicators for impending shifts in distance sensitivity and market size effects. Specifically, we recommend:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Tracking annual changes in PageRank centralization (PRZ) and modularity (MOD) as 1--3 year leading indicators for aggregate distance elasticity changes
    \item Monitoring sector-specific centrality measures (Avg.DCI, Avg.DCO) for anticipating sector-level gravity shifts
    \item Using lacunarity third moment (LL\_m3) as an indicator of network heterogeneity that precedes structural breaks
\end{itemize}

\textit{For supply chain analysis:} The divergence between random and systematic attack resilience (Figure \ref{fig:netall}(c)) provides actionable information for supply chain risk assessment. Supply chains in sectors where this divergence is large face elevated risk from targeted disruptions (geopolitical tensions, sanctions) even if they appear robust to random shocks. The sector-specific causal patterns (Figure \ref{fig:causgravsect}) can identify which industries are most sensitive to network structural changes.

\textit{For international business strategy:} The cluster-specific patterns in gravity coefficient evolution (Figures \ref{fig:gravsect}--\ref{fig:gravproducts}) provide guidance for market selection and expansion timing. Sectors in NDA$_1$ clusters show declining distance barriers, suggesting opportunities for market expansion to more distant destinations, while NDA$_3$ sectors maintain geographic constraints that favor regional concentration.
-->

This study provides systematic evidence of temporal precedence -- based on converging traditional, Bayesian, and machine-learning Granger-style tests, though not structural causal identification -- linking the evolution of trade network topology to subsequent shifts in structural gravity coefficients, using two complementary databases spanning 1995--2022.

## Theoretical Contributions {#subsec:theory_contributions}

Our findings advance international trade theory in three dimensions. \textit{First, bridging gravity and network theories.} We establish a directional, temporal link between the structural gravity framework \citep{anderson2003, yotov2024evolution} and production network theory \citep{acemoglu2012, chaney2014}. The finding that network topology changes Granger-precede gravity coefficient shifts---but rarely vice versa---provides systematic dynamic evidence consistent with the extensive margin (network formation) leading the intensive margin (trade volumes) at the macroeconomic level, extending the static predictions of \citet{melitz2015new} and \citet{helpman2008} to a dynamic setting; as discussed in Section \ref{sec:limitations}, this should be read as temporal-precedence evidence, not structural causal identification.

\textit{Second, a structural account of sectoral heterogeneity in the distance puzzle.} Our most robust finding -- consistent across the aggregate, sectoral, and product-group levels, and confirmed qualitatively by all three causality-testing methods -- is that the distance puzzle \citep{disdier2008, brun2005, yotov2012distance} is not a singular phenomenon but a composition effect: ICT and services sectors exhibit genuine distance compression through network decentralization, while heavy manufacturing maintains geographic constraints through persistent regional modularity. This sector-level decomposition, grounded in the Granger-style temporal-precedence link between modularity and distance elasticity, offers a structural, testable account of why aggregate estimates of the distance puzzle have proven so heterogeneous across studies and samples, though we stop short of claiming it fully resolves the underlying debate.

\textit{Third, linking network fragility to trade frictions.} Our finding that lacunarity moments and fractal dimension Granger-precede gravity coefficient shifts connects the growing literature on trade network resilience \citep{bonadio2021, carvalho2021} to the gravity framework. At the aggregate network level, this heterogeneity-to-gravity link is clearest for GDP elasticities: three of the four lacunarity moments and fractal dimension Granger-precede both origin and destination GDP elasticity, consistent with nonlinear shock amplification mechanisms \citep{baqaee2019macroeconomic}. For distance elasticity, the aggregate-level link is weaker -- none of the four lacunarity moments or fractal dimension Granger-precede the aggregate distance coefficient -- and, consistent with our second contribution, instead emerges at the sectoral and product-group level. This provides both a theoretical mechanism and an empirical tool for understanding how structural vulnerabilities translate into measurable changes in trade frictions, operating principally through economic-mass elasticities at the aggregate level and through distance elasticities at a more granular, sector-specific level.

## Methodological Contributions {#subsec:method_contributions}

Methodologically, we contribute a triangulated causality framework that combines traditional panel Granger tests, Bayesian model comparison, and Random Forest-based variable importance analysis. The machine learning approach reveals nonlinear causal relationships (particularly the role of Trace and Motifs) that linear methods entirely miss, underscoring the value of methodological pluralism in network-gravity analysis.


## Policy Implications {#subsec:policy}

Our findings carry several actionable implications for trade policy design 
and implementation.

\textit{Early Warning System Design.} The documented 1--4 year lead times between network indicator changes and gravity coefficient shifts enable construction of operational early warning systems. We recommend monitoring:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Monthly/Quarterly}: PageRank centralization (PRZ) and modularity (MOD) as short-term (1--2 year) leading indicators
    \item \textbf{Annually}: Lacunarity third moment (LL\_m3) and fractal dimension (FDim) as medium-term (2--4 year) structural change indicators
    \item \textbf{Threshold alerts}: \gls{sres} falling     below \gls{rres} as a vulnerability signal
\end{itemize}

\textit{Sector-Specific Policy Targeting.} The substantial heterogeneity documented across sectors implies differentiated policy approaches:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Digital/ICT sectors} (J61, J62\_63): Prioritize connectivity and efficiency improvements; distance barriers are already low and declining further
    \item \textbf{Heavy manufacturing} (C24--C29): Focus on partner diversification rather than distance reduction; resilience measures show these sectors are vulnerable to hub disruption
    \item \textbf{Agricultural and primary sectors}: Monitor resilience indicators closely; these sectors show strongest coupling between network fragility and distance sensitivity
\end{itemize}

\textit{Regional trade agreement evaluation.} The rising modularity trend (Figure \ref{fig:netall}(a)) combined with its Granger-causal relationship to distance elasticity suggests that trade agreements are not merely redirecting flows but fundamentally restructuring trade costs. Policy evaluation frameworks should incorporate network topology changes as endogenous outcomes rather than treating gravity coefficients as stable parameters.

\textit{Supply Chain Resilience Assessment.} The documented divergence between random (\gls{rres}) and systematic (\gls{sres}) attack resilience provides a quantitative basis for identifying vulnerable sectors. Sectors where 
$\text{SRes} < 0.95 \times \text{RRes}$ should be flagged for supply chain diversification initiatives, as they face elevated risk from targeted disruptions (sanctions, geopolitical tensions) even if robust to random shocks.


# Limitations and Future Work {#sec:limitations}

```{r limitations,results='hide',warning=FALSE,message=FALSE}
PV_ALL_IND  <- rbind(PV_DIST[PV_DIST$level=="individual",],                PV_GDPi[PV_GDPi$level=="individual",],                PV_GDPj[PV_GDPj$level=="individual",])
FDR_ALL_IND <- fdr_correct_panel_results(PV_ALL_IND, level_filter = "individual")
s <- attr(FDR_ALL_IND, "summary")
round(100 * s["n_sig_fdr_q05"] / s["n_sig_raw_alpha01"], 1)      # -> "XX%" Limitations §1

n_robust <- sum(c(PLACEBO_DIST$empirical_p, PLACEBO_GDPi$empirical_p, PLACEBO_GDPj$empirical_p) < 0.05)     # -> "Y of 3 coefficient series"
```


Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, a single common shock would be expected to move all sectors similarly, whereas we document systematic sector- and product-level heterogeneity in the estimated lead-lag pattern (Section \ref{panel-causality-sectoral-and-product-heterogeneity}); this heterogeneity is harder, though not impossible, to reconcile with a single common-shock story than with a sector-specific network-to-gravity channel. We report (Appendix \ref{sec:robustness_fdr_placebo}) a false-discovery-rate-corrected and placebo-benchmarked version of our panel Granger results. After Benjamini--Hochberg correction \citep{benjaminihochberg1995} at the individual sector level (1,008 sector-by-indicator tests per coefficient), only 0 of 39 raw-significant distance relationships and 0 of 44 raw-significant destination-\gls{gdp} relationships survive at $q=0.05$ (2 of 45 for origin \gls{gdp}); at the pooled panel level (12 sector-fixed-effects tests per coefficient), by contrast, 11 of 12 origin-\gls{gdp} and 8 of 12 destination-\gls{gdp} tests remain significant at $q=0.05$. A complementary circular-shift placebo test \citep{theiler1992surrogate} shows that the observed number of significant sector-level pairs (117 for distance, 137 for origin \gls{gdp}, 130 for destination \gls{gdp}) exceeds the 95th percentile of its placebo null distribution in every case (99, 86, and 114, respectively; empirical $p<0.01$ for all three). Taken together, these diagnostics indicate that individual sector-by-indicator claims should be treated cautiously -- most do not survive correction for testing many sector/variable/lag combinations -- but that the pooled, aggregate-level pattern of network-to-gravity predictability is not solely an artefact of multiple testing. By construction, neither diagnostic can distinguish a genuine network-to-gravity mechanism from an unobserved common driver with a similar lag structure; we therefore describe our results throughout as evidence of robust temporal precedence rather than as establishing a causal mechanism (see the revised framing in Section \ref{sec:introduction} and the Conclusion). Future work could employ instrumental-variable approaches (e.g., plausibly exogenous shocks to specific trade corridors) or quasi-experimental designs (e.g., staggered regional-trade-agreement entry into force) to strengthen causal identification. 

Second, the relatively short time series (26--28 annual observations) limits the power of causality tests, increases sensitivity to lag-order choice, and raises the risk of spurious findings when many sector/product/lag combinations are tested; it also limits the ability to detect long-horizon relationships or multiple structural breaks. We now report, alongside our main results, a false-discovery-rate-corrected version of the panel Granger tests and a circular-shift placebo benchmark that directly quantify this risk rather than relying on cross-method triangulation alone. Triangulation across traditional, Bayesian, and machine-learning approaches remains informative about the robustness of a finding to modelling choices, but, as the reviewer correctly notes, it cannot by itself overcome the fundamental power limitation of a 26--28-year panel. As longer series become available, extended analysis could identify regime-specific patterns and long-run equilibrium relationships with adequately powered tests.

Third, our analysis treats sectors and product groups as independent units, ignoring input-output linkages that may propagate network effects across categories. Future work integrating the multiplex structure of inter-sectoral trade could reveal how network changes in upstream sectors cascade to downstream gravity coefficients.

Fourth, we focus on aggregate country-level networks, abstracting from firm-level heterogeneity that may be important for understanding micro-level mechanisms. Firm-level trade data, where available, could enable analysis of how network position of individual firms relates to their distance sensitivity.

Fifth, structural gravity specification. As explained in Section \ref{sec:gravity_spec}, a specification with country-pair fixed effects is not compatible with our object of interest -- year-specific distance and GDP elasticities -- because distance is time-invariant per pair and a pair fixed effect would saturate a design with one observation per pair per year; exporter- or importer-year fixed effects are similarly infeasible here, because within a single year they would be collinear with the very GDP elasticities $\beta_{o,t}$ and $\beta_{d,t}$ that we aim to estimate. Instead, Equation \eqref{eq:gravity} includes nine bilateral controls from the CEPII Gravity database \citep{conte2022cepii} directly in every year-specific cross-section: common official and ethnic language, contiguity, colonial history, common legal origin, joint FTA/WTO membership, and EU membership of either partner (Section \ref{sec:gravity_spec}). These bilateral controls absorb considerable time-invariant bilateral heterogeneity, but, as discussed in Section \ref{subsec:identification}, they cannot substitute for the country-specific multilateral resistance terms that exporter- or importer-year fixed effects would otherwise capture. This specification also still falls short of the full structural-gravity toolkit recommended by \citet{larch2025estimating} for panel gravity estimation, and it does not explicitly model firm-level heterogeneity \citep{helpman2008, melitz2015new}. Future work should extend our framework to incorporate the full structural gravity toolkit, potentially using the constrained \gls{ppml} approach of \citet{larch2025estimating} to separate genuine distance-elasticity evolution from changes in correlated bilateral factors.

Sixth, macro-level vs. firm-level analysis. Our analysis operates at the country-sector and country-product level, which necessarily aggregates over firm-level heterogeneity. While \citet{chaney2014} provides the theoretical link between firm-level decisions and network topology, our data do not allow direct observation of the firm-level mechanisms underlying the documented Granger-causal relationships. Future work using firm-level customs data could test whether the extensive margin dynamics we identify at the macro level are indeed driven by firm entry/exit patterns.


Finally, future work should explore the forecasting value of network indicators more formally through out-of-sample prediction exercises, and investigate whether the identified relationships remain stable during periods of major disruption (such as the COVID-19 pandemic) or exhibit structural breaks that would limit their predictive utility.

## Forecasting of Elasticies {#app:forecast}

Figure \ref{fig:gravsect} presents the \gls{gnda}-identified clusters of industrial sectors based on the temporal similarity of their gravity coefficients, with forecasts to 2030. The clustering uses Spearman correlation as the similarity measure. 

```{r gravsect,echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,fig.align='center',fig.cap="Coefficients of gravity models in time (forecast wth ARIMA, 95% confidence interval, based on OECD-ICIO database)",fig.subcap=c("Distance","Origin","Destination"),fig.ncol=3,out.width = '33%',fig.pos="H"}

set.seed(2)

start<-2021
end<-2030
BAYESIAN <- FALSE

# Distance 

tmp<-t(grav_sect_time$beta["dist",,])
NDA<-ndr(tmp,cor_method = 2)
NDAdist<-NDA
NDAdist_sect<-NDAdist

for (i in 1:NDA$factors){
  if (i==1){
    data<-cbind(as.numeric(rownames(tmp)),rowWeightedMeans(tmp[,NDA$membership==i],w=abs(NDA$loadings[cbind(seq_along(NDA$membership),NDA$membership)][NDA$membership==i])))
  }else{
    data<-cbind(data,rowWeightedMeans(tmp[,NDA$membership==i],w=abs(NDA$loadings[cbind(seq_along(NDA$membership),NDA$membership)][NDA$membership==i])))
  }
}
data<-as.data.frame(data)
colnames(data)[1]<-"Year"
for (i in 1:NDA$factors){
  colnames(data)[i+1]<-paste("NDA",i," (",paste(colnames(tmp)[NDA$membership==i],collapse = ', '),")",sep="")
}
## ARIMA
fit<-autoarima(data[,-1],bayesian = BAYESIAN)
fc<-forecasts(fit,bayesian = BAYESIAN)
fc_df<-astibble(fc)
for (i in 1:length(fc[[1]]$mean)){
    forec<-fc[[1]]$mean
    for (j in 2:length(fc)){
        forec<-cbind(forec,fc[[j]]$mean)
    }
}
forec<-cbind(start:end,forec)
colnames(forec)<-colnames(data)
data<-rbind(data,forec)
data_melted<-melt(data,id.vars = "Year")

## Forecast
data_melted$`Lo 95`<-NA
data_melted$`Hi 95`<-NA

for (j in 2:ncol(data)){
    data_melted[(data_melted$variable %in% colnames(data)[j]) & (data_melted$Year %in% start:end),4]<-fc[[j-1]]$lower
    data_melted[(data_melted$variable %in% colnames(data)[j]) & (data_melted$Year %in% start:end),5]<-fc[[j-1]]$upper
}

data_melted <- data_melted %>%
  mutate(variable = str_wrap(variable, width = 20))

ggplot(data_melted, aes(x = Year, y = value, color = variable)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = value)) +
  geom_line(size = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = `Lo 95`, ymax = `Hi 95`), fill = "grey80") +
  geom_point(aes(y = value)) +
  labs(title = "",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Distance coefficient",
       color = "Industries") +
  theme(legend.position="bottom")

write.xlsx(data_melted,file="output/FIG03a_FORECAST_TRAD_OECD_sect_dist.xlsx",showNA = FALSE)

For distance coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravsect}(a)), three clusters emerge: NDA$_1$ (23 sectors) includes service-oriented and domestic-focused industries such as agriculture (A01\_02), accommodation (I), real estate (L), and public services (O, P, Q), exhibiting distance coefficients around $-0.55$ to $-0.45$; NDA$_2$ (12 sectors) comprises resource-intensive and manufacturing industries including mining (B05\_06, B07\_08), food products (C10T12), chemicals (C20), and wholesale trade (G), with coefficients between $-0.50$ and $-0.45$; NDA$_3$ (9 sectors) contains technology-intensive manufacturing such as paper products (C17\_18), electronics (C26), electrical equipment (C27), and telecommunications (J61), showing the steepest decline in distance sensitivity from $-0.60$ to $-0.45$.

For origin \gls{gdp} coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravsect}(b)), NDA$_1$ (26 sectors) groups export-capacity-sensitive industries including chemicals (C20), machinery (C28), and professional services (M); NDA$_2$ (10 sectors) contains labor-intensive sectors such as textiles (C13T15), utilities (D, E), and education (P); NDA$_3$ (8 sectors) includes capital-intensive industries like basic metals (C24), electronics (C26), and land transport (H49).

For destination \gls{gdp} coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravsect}(c)), NDA$_1$ (24 sectors) encompasses market-access-sensitive industries including most manufacturing sectors and business services; NDA$_2$ (13 sectors) contains domestically-oriented services such as accommodation (I), real estate (L), and public administration (O); NDA$_3$ (7 sectors) groups transport and electronics sectors including water transport (H50), warehousing (H52), and motor vehicles (C29).

Figure \ref{fig:gravprodgroup} displays the \gls{gnda}-identified clusters of product groups (HS-2 level, 97 categories) from the \gls{cepii}-\gls{baci} database, based on temporal patterns in gravity coefficients.  

```{r gravprodgroup,echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,fig.align='center',fig.cap="Coefficients of gravity models for product groups in time (forecast wth ARIMA, 95% confidence interval, based on BACI-CEPII database)",fig.subcap=c("Distance","Origin","Destination"),fig.ncol=3,out.width = '33%',fig.pos="H"}

set.seed(2)

start<-2023
end<-2030
BAYESIAN=FALSE


# Distance 

tmp<-t(var_products_time_20["dist",,-29])
NDA<-ndr(tmp,cor_method = 2)
NDAdist<-NDA
NDAdist_pg<-NDAdist
for (i in 1:NDA$factors){
  if (i==1){
    data<-cbind(as.numeric(rownames(tmp)),rowWeightedMeans(tmp[,NDA$membership==i],w=abs(NDA$loadings[cbind(seq_along(NDA$membership),NDA$membership)][NDA$membership==i])))
  }else{
    data<-cbind(data,rowWeightedMeans(tmp[,NDA$membership==i],w=abs(NDA$loadings[cbind(seq_along(NDA$membership),NDA$membership)][NDA$membership==i])))
  }
}
data<-as.data.frame(data)
colnames(data)[1]<-"Year"
for (i in 1:NDA$factors){
  colnames(data)[i+1]<-paste("NDA",i," (",paste(colnames(tmp)[NDA$membership==i],collapse = ', '),")",sep="")
}
## ARIMA
fit<-autoarima(data[,-1],bayesian = BAYESIAN)
fc<-forecasts(fit,h=8,bayesian = BAYESIAN)
fc_df<-astibble(fc,index = start:end)
for (i in 1:length(fc[[1]]$mean)){
    forec<-fc[[1]]$mean
    for (j in 2:length(fc)){
        forec<-cbind(forec,fc[[j]]$mean)
    }
}
forec<-cbind(start:end,forec)
colnames(forec)<-colnames(data)
data<-rbind(data,forec)
data_melted<-melt(data,id.vars = "Year")

## Forecast
data_melted$`Lo 95`<-NA
data_melted$`Hi 95`<-NA

for (j in 2:ncol(data)){
    data_melted[(data_melted$variable %in% colnames(data)[j]) & (data_melted$Year %in% start:end),4]<-fc[[j-1]]$lower
    data_melted[(data_melted$variable %in% colnames(data)[j]) & (data_melted$Year %in% start:end),5]<-fc[[j-1]]$upper
}

data_melted <- data_melted %>%
  mutate(variable = str_wrap(variable, width = 20))

ggplot(data_melted, aes(x = Year, y = value, color = variable)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = value)) +
  geom_line(size = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = `Lo 95`, ymax = `Hi 95`), fill = "grey80") +
  geom_point(aes(y = value)) +
  labs(title = "",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Distance coefficient",
       color = "Product groups") +
  theme(legend.position="bottom")

write.xlsx(data_melted,file="output/FIG04a_FORECAST_TRAD_CEPII_pg_dist.xlsx",showNA = FALSE)

<!--
Figure \ref{fig:gravprodgroup} shows that
*`r as.character(english(NDAdist$factors))`* clusters can be defined for
distance, *`r as.character(english(NDAGDPi$factors))`* cluster for
origin and *`r as.character(english(NDAGDPi$factors))`* clusters for
destination gravity coefficients.-->

For distance coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravprodgroup}(a)), three clusters are identified: NDA$_1$ (49 product groups) includes manufactured goods such as vehicles (87), machinery (84), electrical equipment (85), textiles (55--59), and footwear (64), showing distance coefficients stabilizing around $-0.10$; NDA$_2$ (41 product groups) comprises primary products and intermediates including live animals (01), minerals (25--27), base metals (72--76), and paper (48), with coefficients around $-0.15$; NDA$_3$ (6 product groups) contains specific categories including fertilizers (28, 29), cork products (53, 54), lead (78), and ships (89), exhibiting the highest distance sensitivity near $-0.20$.

For origin \gls{gdp} coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravprodgroup}(b)), NDA$_1$ (47 groups) includes differentiated manufactures; NDA$_2$ (25 groups) contains agricultural and food products; NDA$_3$ (24 groups) comprises raw materials and standardized intermediates.

For destination \gls{gdp} coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravprodgroup}(c)), NDA$_1$ (61 groups) encompasses most consumer and industrial goods; NDA$_2$ (35 groups) includes commodities and specialized equipment.

```{r, include=FALSE}
l <- split(rownames(NDAdist$loadings), NDAdist$membership)

out <- paste(
  mapply(function(n, x) paste0(n, ": ", paste(x, collapse = ", ")),
         names(l), l),
  collapse = "; "
)
write(paste("The identified product group IDs within clusters of distance coefficient", out),file="output/NDAdist_pg.txt")
```

<!--Figure \ref{fig:gravsubprodgroup} shows that
*`r as.character(english(NDAdist$factors))`* clusters can be defined for
distance, *`r as.character(english(NDAGDPi$factors))`* cluster for
origin and *`r as.character(english(NDAGDPi$factors))`* clusters for
destination gravity coefficients.-->

For distance coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravsubprodgroup}(a)), three clusters emerge with coefficients ranging from $-0.30$ (NDA$_3$) to $-0.10$ (NDA$_1$). NDA$_1$ (49 subgroups) includes specialized products such as dairy (0401), nuclear reactors (8401--8402), and motorcycles (8711); NDA$_2$ (approximately 350 subgroups) contains diverse intermediates including live animals, vegetables, textiles, and machinery parts; NDA$_3$ (approximately 200 subgroups) comprises bulk commodities, ores, and basic chemicals.

For origin \gls{gdp} coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravsubprodgroup}(b)), four clusters are identified (NDA$_1$ through NDA$_4$), with coefficients ranging from 0.20 to 0.40, reflecting varying degrees of supply-side economic scale effects across product categories.

For destination \gls{gdp} coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravsubprodgroup}(c)), three clusters show destination market size elasticities between 0.15 and 0.35, with consumer goods generally exhibiting higher demand-side \gls{gdp} sensitivity than industrial intermediates.

         names(l), l),
  collapse = "; "
)

write(paste("The identified product subgroup IDs within clusters of distance coefficient", out),file="output/NDAdist_psg.txt")

<!--Figure \ref{fig:gravproducts} shows that
*`r as.character(english(NDAdist$factors))`* clusters can be defined for
distance, *`r as.character(english(NDAGDPi$factors))`* cluster for
origin and *`r as.character(english(NDAGDPi$factors))`* clusters for
destination gravity coefficients.-->

For distance coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravproducts}(a)), three clusters are identified: NDA$_1$ exhibits the lowest distance sensitivity (around $-0.15$), containing differentiated manufactured products; NDA$_2$ shows intermediate sensitivity (around $-0.20$), comprising semi-processed goods; NDA$_3$ displays the highest distance sensitivity (around $-0.30$), including bulk commodities and weight-sensitive products.

For origin \gls{gdp} coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravproducts}(b)), three clusters span the range from 0.25 to 0.45, with NDA$_1$ capturing products where exporter economic size strongly influences trade volumes, typically capital-intensive manufactures.

For destination \gls{gdp} coefficients (Figure \ref{fig:gravproducts}(c)), three clusters range from 0.20 to 0.30, with consumer goods and final products (NDA$_1$) showing higher destination \gls{gdp} elasticity than intermediate inputs (NDA$_2$ and NDA$_3$).

Across all aggregation levels (Figures \ref{fig:gravprodgroup}--\ref{fig:gravproducts}), a consistent pattern emerges: the number of identified clusters ranges from two to four, with three being most common, suggesting that trade products naturally partition into distinct categories based on their sensitivity to distance and economic mass.

```{r, include=FALSE}
l <- split(rownames(NDAdist$loadings), NDAdist$membership)
names(l) <- paste0("NDA$_", 1:NDAdist$factors, "$")
out <- paste(
  mapply(function(n, x) paste0(n, ": ", paste(x, collapse = ", ")),
         names(l), l),
  collapse = "; "
)

write(paste("The identified product IDs within clusters of distance coefficient", out),file="output/NDAdist_prod.txt")
```

The correspondence between product-level clusters (BACI-CEPII) and sectoral clusters (OECD-ICIO) is examined in Section \ref{subsec:theory_implications}, where we discuss how product categories map to industrial sectors and whether their network-gravity relationships exhibit consistent patterns.

Figure \ref{fig:correlationsect} displays Spearman correlations between gravity coefficients and selected network indicators disaggregated by industrial sector, revealing substantial heterogeneity across industries. Cells in Figure \ref{fig:correlationsect} (and in Figures \ref{fig:correlationsectnda}--\ref{fig:correlationprodnda} below, which use the same convention) are set to zero, and therefore appear white, whenever the underlying Spearman correlation is not statistically significant at the 5\% level; only coloured (non-white) cells represent correlations distinguishable from zero.

```{r correlationsect,echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,fig.align='center',fig.cap="Spearman's correlation between gravity coefficients and network-level (and aggregated node-level) indicators ",fig.pos="H",fig.ncol=3,out.height="30%",out.width="33%",fig.subcap=c("Industries: A01-02--C24","Industries: C25--H52","Industries: H53--S")}
colH=colorRamp2(c(-1,0,1),c("darkred","white","darkblue"))
X<-var_sect_time[-c(1:12,25),,]
Y<-grav_sect_time$beta[1:3,,]
ht_list = NULL  ## Heatmap(...) + NULL gives you a HeatmapList object
corSig <- function(Ymat, Xmat, alpha = 0.05) {
  ct <- corr.test(t(Ymat), t(Xmat), method = "spearman",adjust = "fdr")
  r <- ct$r
  r[ct$p.adj > alpha] <- 0
  r
}
for(i in 1:15) {
    ht_list = ht_list %v% Heatmap(corSig(Y[,i,], X[,i,]),show_heatmap_legend = FALSE,row_title =dimnames(X)[[2]][[i]],row_title_gp = gpar(fontsize = 4),row_names_gp = gpar(fontsize = 4),col = colH,column_names_gp = gpar(fontsize = 6),height = unit(5,"mm"))
    m<-cor(t(Y[,i,]),t(X[,i,]),method="spearman")
    p<-corr.test(t(Y[,i,]),t(X[,i,]),method="spearman",adjust = "fdr")$p.adj
    rownames(p)<-rownames(m)<-paste(rownames(m),dimnames(X)[[2]][[i]],sep=", sect:")
    if (i==1){
      M<-m
      P<-p
    }else {
      M<-rbind(M,m)
      P<-rbind(P,p)
    } 
}
draw(ht_list,row_title="Industries/sectors",ht_gap=unit(0.5,"mm"))

The correlation patterns vary considerably across sectors. For most manufacturing sectors (C20--C30), the ordering of correlations follows: destination \gls{gdp} shows the strongest positive correlation with centrality measures, followed by origin \gls{gdp}, while distance exhibits negative correlations. Service sectors (K, L, M, N) display similar patterns but with generally weaker magnitudes. Resource extraction sectors (B05\_06, B07\_08) show distinctive patterns where distance correlations are less negative than in manufacturing, suggesting lower distance sensitivity in raw material trade. The lacunarity and fractal dimension indicators show sector-specific patterns: technology-intensive sectors (C26, J61) exhibit stronger correlations with LL\_m2 and LL\_m3 than traditional manufacturing sectors.

Figure \ref{fig:correlationprod} presents Spearman correlations between gravity coefficients and network indicators for each of the 97 product groups in the \gls{cepii}-\gls{baci} database.

```{r correlationprod,echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,fig.align='center',fig.cap="Spearman's correlation between gravity coefficients and network-level (and aggregated node-level) indicators ",fig.pos="H",fig.ncol=6,out.height="30%",out.width="16%",fig.subcap=c("Product groups: 01--16","Product groups: 17--32","Product groups: 33--48","Product groups: 49--64","Product groups: 65--81","Product groups: 83--97")}

ht_list = NULL  ## Heatmap(...) + NULL gives you a HeatmapList object
corSigT <- function(Ymat, Xmat_ready, alpha = 0.05) {
  ct <- corr.test(t(Ymat), Xmat_ready, method = "spearman",adjust="fdr")
  r <- ct$r
  r[ct$p.adj > alpha] <- 0
  r
}
for(i in 1:16) {
  x<-t(X[,i,])
  if (sum(is.na(x))<200){
    x[is.na(x)]<-0
    ht_list = ht_list %v% Heatmap(corSigT(Y[,i,],x),show_heatmap_legend = FALSE,row_title =dimnames(X)[[2]][[i]],row_title_gp = gpar(fontsize = 4),row_names_gp = gpar(fontsize = 4),col = colH,column_names_gp = gpar(fontsize = 6),height = unit(5,"mm"))
    m<-cor(t(Y[,i,]),x,method="spearman")
    p<-corr.test(t(Y[,i,]),x,method="spearman",adjust = "fdr")$p.adj
    rownames(p)<-rownames(m)<-paste(rownames(m),dimnames(X)[[2]][[i]],sep=", product:")
    if (i==1){
      M<-m
      P<-p
    }else {
        M<-rbind(M,m)
        P<-rbind(P,p)
    } 
  }
}
draw(ht_list,row_title="Product groups",ht_gap=unit(0.5,"mm"))

        P<-rbind(P,p)
    } 
}}
draw(ht_list,row_title="Product groups",ht_gap=unit(1,"mm"))

write.xlsx(M,file="output/FIG11_COR_NETPROD_CEPII.xlsx",showNA = FALSE,sheetName = "COR",append = FALSE)
write.xlsx(P,file="output/FIG11_COR_NETPROD_CEPII.xlsx",showNA = FALSE,sheetName = "P-VALUE",append = TRUE)
```

Substantial heterogeneity emerges across product groups. The lacunarity moments display strongly product-specific patterns: LL\_m3 and LL\_m4 correlations range from about $-0.96$ to $0.92$ across the 86 product groups for which the correlation could be computed, confirming that the relationship between network heterogeneity and gravity parameters depends strongly on product characteristics. Resilience indicators (\gls{rres}, \gls{sres}) are, on average, negatively---rather than positively---correlated with distance coefficients: 77% of product groups (66 of 86) show a negative RRes--distance correlation (mean $r=-0.29$) and 76% (65 of 86) show a negative SRes--distance correlation (mean $r=-0.33$), so for most product groups a more resilient network structure coincides with higher, rather than lower, distance sensitivity in trade.

## Employed Gravity Models {#sec:calcgrav}

Let $T_{ij,t}$ denote bilateral trade from origin country $i$ to
destination country $j$ in period $t$, let $GDP_{i,t}$ and $GDP_{j,t}$
be the corresponding \glspl{gdp}, and let $dist_{ij}$ be the
great-circle distance between $i$ and $j$ (time-invariant). A
parsimonious, multiplicative gravity baseline with time-varying
elasticities is \begin{equation}
T_{ij,t} = A_t \cdot GDP_{i,t}^{,\beta_{o,t}} \cdot GDP_{j,t}^{,\beta_{d,t}} \cdot  dist_{ij}^{-\gamma_t} \cdot \varepsilon_{ij,t},
\label{eq:grav_mult}
\end{equation}

\noindent where $A_t>0$ is a time-specific scale, $\beta_{o,t}$ and
$\beta_{d,t}$ are the output elasticities at origin and destination, and
$\gamma_t$ is the distance elasticity (“trade-cost elasticity of
distance”). In log-linear form, \begin{equation}
\ln T_{ij,t} = \alpha_t + \beta_{o,t},\ln GDP_{i,t} + \beta_{d,t},\ln GDP_{j,t} - \gamma_t,\ln dist_{ij} + u_{ij,t},
\label{eq:grav_log}
\end{equation}

Estimation can proceed separately for each $t$ (sequence of
cross-sections) to obtain a time series
$\{\widehat{\beta}_{o,t},\widehat{\beta}_{d,t},\widehat{\gamma}_{t}\}$,
or in a panel by interacting regressors with time dummies to allow
unrestricted time-variation in elasticities.

Richer specifications often augment \eqref{eq:grav_log} with additional
covariates (contiguity, common language, historical ties, trade
agreements, multilateral-resistance terms), improving in-sample fit and
structural interpretation; see, e.g., @anderson2003, @headmayer2014, and
@anderson2011. However, such covariates are frequently correlated with
$\ln dist_{i,j}$, and—especially in short samples—the resulting
multicollinearity can change and potentially distort the estimated
distance elasticity $\gamma_t$. Because our objective is to track the
evolution of the core elasticities
$\{\beta_{o,t},\beta_{d,t},\gamma_{t}\}$, we weigh this multicollinearity
risk against the value of additional covariates when finalizing our
specification. The model we actually estimate throughout this paper,
Equation \eqref{eq:gravity} (Section \ref{sec:gravity_spec}), extends
\eqref{eq:grav_log} with nine CEPII bilateral controls $D_{m,ij}$
\citep{conte2022cepii} in place of the exporter-/importer-year or
country-pair fixed effects that this year-by-year cross-sectional design
cannot otherwise accommodate (Section \ref{sec:gravity_spec}). Appendix
\ref{app:ols_ppml_comparison} empirically revisits the multicollinearity
concern raised above: across all five databases, the nine bilateral
controls show markedly weaker sign and joint-significance agreement
between \gls{ols} and \gls{ppml} than the three core elasticities do,
consistent with their being static bilateral dummies rather than a full
fixed-effects structure.

Interpretation of time-variation in coefficients. The sequence
$\{\gamma_t\}$ captures how the “penalty of distance” changes over time.
Changes in the output elasticities reflect evolving size effects on bilateral trade. The resulting coefficient time series enables time series analyses such as trend estimation, structural break detection, volatility comparisons across regimes, and event studies.

Disaggregation by product $k$, product group, or sector $s$ reveals heterogeneity in how distance and size effects evolve across technologies, value chain positions, and demand elasticities:

\begin{equation}
\ln T_{ij,t}^{(k)} = \alpha_t^{(k)} + \beta_{o,t}^{(k)} \ln GDP_{i,t} + \beta_{d,t}^{(k)} \ln GDP_{j,t} - \gamma_t^{(k)} \ln dist_{ij} + u_{ij,t}^{(k)}.
\end{equation}

Throughout this paper we estimate the fuller specification
\eqref{eq:gravity} (Section \ref{sec:gravity_spec}) by \gls{ppml} on
trade in levels rather than \eqref{eq:grav_log} by \gls{ols} on
$\ln T_{ij,t}$, for the reasons detailed in Section
\ref{sec:ppml_robust}. Regardless of which bilateral controls are
included, our object of interest remains the same three core
elasticities $\{\beta_{o,t},\beta_{d,t},\gamma_{t}\}$: the “penalty of
distance” $\gamma_t$ and the origin/destination output elasticities
$\beta_{o,t}$, $\beta_{d,t}$.

## Robustness Check {#sec:ppml_robust}

To address concerns about heteroskedasticity and zero trade flows \citep{SantosSilvaTenreyro2006, santos2011}, we estimate every year-specific, product/sector-specific cross-section of Equation \eqref{eq:gravity} (Section \ref{sec:gravity_spec}) by \gls{ppml} rather than by log-linearized \gls{ols} on $\ln(Trade_{ij,t}+1)$. \gls{ppml} is robust to heteroskedasticity and lets zero-trade observations enter the estimation naturally, rather than being dropped or ad hoc adjusted \citep{SantosSilvaTenreyro2006}. As explained in Section \ref{sec:gravity_spec}, country-pair fixed effects cannot be added to this year-by-year cross-sectional design without saturating the data, and exporter- or importer-year fixed effects cannot be added without absorbing the GDP elasticities $\beta_{o,t}^{k}$ and $\beta_{d,t}^{k}$ that Equation \eqref{eq:gravity} is designed to estimate; the nine CEPII bilateral controls $D_{m,ij}$ \citep{conte2022cepii} take the place of either type of fixed effect.

Appendix \ref{app:ols_ppml_comparison} reports the full empirical comparison between the \gls{ols} and \gls{ppml} estimates of Equation \eqref{eq:gravity} for every database, year, and product/sector, confirming that our main findings are not an artefact of the choice of estimator.

## Comparison of OLS and PPML Estimates for the Bilateral Control Variables {#app:ols_ppml_comparison}

Section \ref{sec:ppml_robust} explains why we estimate Equation \eqref{eq:gravity} (Section \ref{sec:gravity_spec}) by \gls{ppml} rather than by \gls{ols}; here we report the full empirical comparison between the two estimators. For every year $t$, product/sector $k$, and database, Equation \eqref{eq:gravity} is re-estimated both by \gls{ppml} on trade in levels (our baseline, reported throughout the main text) and by \gls{ols} on $\ln(Trade_{ij,t}^{k}+1)$, using paired estimation scripts that share the same underlying \texttt{gravity\_engine.r} routine and differ only in the link function and the treatment of zero-trade observations: \texttt{ICIO\_AGG\_PPML.r}/\texttt{ICIO\_AGG\_OLS.r} (aggregate OECD-ICIO), \texttt{ICIO\_SECT\_PPML.r}/\texttt{ICIO\_SECT\_OLS.r} (sectoral OECD-ICIO), and \texttt{CEPII\_PG\_PPML.r}/\texttt{CEPII\_PG\_OLS.r}, \texttt{CEPII\_PSG\_PPML.r}/\texttt{CEPII\_PSG\_OLS.r}, \texttt{CEPII\_PROD\_PPML.r}/\texttt{CEPII\_PROD\_OLS.r} (BACI-CEPII product groups, subgroups, and products).

For $\beta_{o,t}^{k}$, $\beta_{d,t}^{k}$, and $\gamma_t^{k}$ we compute the Spearman rank correlation between the two series, following the procedure of Section \ref{sec:ppml_robust}. For the nine $\delta_{m,t}^{k}$ bilateral-control coefficients -- which, as noted in Section \ref{sec:constructed_databases}, are not carried forward as $Y$ variables into the network-causality analysis -- rather than reproducing nine additional coefficient-by-year panels in the main text, we report, for each control $D_m$, the share of year-by-product/sector cells in which the \gls{ols} and \gls{ppml} estimates agree in sign and the share for which both are statistically significant at the 5\% level.

Pooled across all five databases, years, and products/sectors, the three core elasticities agree in sign between \gls{ols} and \gls{ppml} in 87.8--98.3\% of cells and are jointly significant at the 5\% level under both estimators in 52.5--91.3\% of cells. The nine bilateral controls agree in sign in only 62.6--76.9\% of cells and are jointly significant under both in just 6.2--38.3\% of cells -- the expected pattern for static bilateral dummies estimated without country-pair or country-year fixed effects.

## Construction of Temporal Multilayer Trade Network Graphs {#sec:dynamicnet}

We model trade as a time-indexed family of weighted, directed multilayer
graphs with fixed country and layer sets and time-varying edge weights.

Let $\mathcal{V}=\{1,\dots,N\}$ denote the set of countries (nodes),
$\mathcal{L}=\{1,\dots,L\}$ the set of layers (product groups or
sectors), and $\mathcal{T}=\{t_1,\dots,t_T\}$ the set of discrete time
points (years). Nodes and layers are time-invariant; only edge weights
vary with $t\in\mathcal{T}$.

\begin{equation}
\mathcal{M} \;=\; \big\{\, \mathcal{M}^t = (\mathcal{V},\mathcal{L},\mathcal{E}^t,w^t) \,\big\}_{t\in\mathcal{T}},
\label{eq:temporal-family}
\end{equation}

\noindent where
$\mathcal{E}^t \subseteq \mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L}$
is the edge set at time $t$, and

\begin{equation}
w^t:\;\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{L}\times\mathcal{L}\to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}, \qquad
(i,j,I,J)\mapsto w_{ij}^{I\to J}(t)
\label{eq:weight-function}
\end{equation}

\noindent assigns a nonnegative trade volume from origin country $i$ and
origin layer $I$ to destination country $j$ and destination layer $J$ at
time $t$. Directedness is encoded by the ordered pair $(i,j)$. The edge
set can be written as \begin{equation}
\mathcal{E}^t \;=\; \big\{\, (i,j,I,J)\in \mathcal{V}^2\times \mathcal{L}^2 \;:\; w_{ij}^{I\to J}(t) > 0 \,\big\}.
\label{eq:edge-set}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
A(t)_{i j I J} \;=\; w_{ij}^{I\to J}(t),
\label{eq:adjacency-tensor}
\end{equation} i.e.,
$A(t)\in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{\,N\times N\times L\times L}$.
Equivalently, the $NL\times NL$ supra-adjacency matrix $S(t)$ indexed by
pairs $(i,I)$ and $(j,J)$ is

\begin{equation}
S(t)_{(i,I),(j,J)} \;=\; w_{ij}^{I\to J}(t), \qquad S(t)\in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{\,NL\times NL}.
\label{eq:supra}
\end{equation}

\noindent Writing $S(t)$ in $L\times L$ blocks of size $N\times N$
yields \begin{equation}
S(t) \;=\;
\begin{bmatrix}
B_{11}(t) & B_{12}(t) & \cdots & B_{1L}(t)\\
B_{21}(t) & B_{22}(t) & \cdots & B_{2L}(t)\\
\vdots    & \vdots    & \ddots & \vdots   \\
B_{L1}(t) & B_{L2}(t) & \cdots & B_{LL}(t)
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
B_{I J}(t) \;=\; \big[w_{ij}^{I\to J}(t)\big]_{i,j=1}^N.
\label{eq:block-structure}
\end{equation}

The temporal network is the sequence with fixed dimensions and
time-varying entries: \begin{equation}
\big\{ S(t) \big\}_{t\in\mathcal{T}}, \qquad N,L \text{ fixed}, \ \ S(t) \text{ varies over } t.
\label{eq:temporal-sequence}
\end{equation} No inter-time edges are assumed by default; dynamic
processes can be modelled by introducing inter-slice coupling between
$(i,I,t)$ and $(i,I,t+1)$ if required.

\acrshort{dci} & \acrlong{dci} & $\text{DCI}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{N} a_{ji}$ & Number of incoming trade connections; measures import partner diversity \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{dco} & \acrlong{dco} & $\text{DCO}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{N} a_{ij}$ & Number of outgoing trade connections; measures export partner diversity \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{sci} & \acrlong{sci} & $\text{SCI}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_{ji}$ & Total value of imports; captures import volume from all partners \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{sco} & \acrlong{sco} & $\text{SCO}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_{ij}$ & Total value of exports; captures export volume to all partners \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{bc} & \acrlong{bc} & $\text{BC}_i = \sum_{s \neq i \neq t} \frac{\sigma_{st}(i)}{\sigma_{st}}$ & Fraction of shortest trade paths passing through node $i$; measures brokerage role \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{ec} & \acrlong{ec} & $\mathbf{Ax} = \lambda_{\max} \mathbf{x}$, where $\text{EC}_i = x_i$ & Centrality based on connections to other central nodes; captures prestige \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{kc} & \acrlong{kc} & $\text{KC}_i = \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{N} a_{ij} \text{KC}_j + \beta$ & Weighted sum of direct and indirect connections; accounts for all path lengths \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{hc} & \acrlong{hc} & $\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{a}$; $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{h}$ (iterative) & Authority of nodes pointed to; identifies countries exporting to important importers \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{ac} & \acrlong{ac} & $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{h}$; $\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{a}$ (iterative) & Authority of nodes pointing in; identifies countries importing from important exporters \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{prc} & \acrlong{prc} & $\text{PRC}_i = (1-d) + d \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i^{\text{in}}} \frac{\text{PRC}_j}{\text{DCO}_j}$ & Recursive prestige measure; importance weighted by partners' importance \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{kcr} & \acrlong{kcr} & $\max\{k : \text{DCI}_i \geq k \text{ and } \text{DCO}_i \geq k\}$ & Maximal subgraph where all nodes have degree $\geq k$; identifies core-periphery structure \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{ecc} & \acrlong{ecc} & $\text{ECC}_i = \max_{j} d(i,j)$ & Maximum shortest path distance from node $i$; measures remoteness \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{lev} & \acrlong{lev} & $\text{LEV}_i = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}_i|(|\mathcal{N}_i|-1)} \sum_{j,k \in \mathcal{N}_i, j \neq k} \frac{1}{d_{jk}}$ & Efficiency of subgraph of node $i$'s neighbors; measures local connectivity robustness \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{rec} & \acrlong{rec} & $REC=\frac{\sum_{i\neq j}a_{ij}\cdot a_{ji}}{\sum_{i\neq j} a_{ij}}$ &  The tendency of pairs of nodes to form mutual connections. It is defined as the proportion of links that are bidirectional relative to the total number of links in the network. \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{ll} & \acrlong{ll} & $\text{LL}_i = \frac{\langle r_i^2 \rangle}{\langle r_i \rangle^2}$ & Local heterogeneity of trade connections; measures irregularity around node $i$ \\

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\noindent \textbf{Notation:} $N$ = number of nodes (countries); $a_{ij}$
= adjacency matrix element (1 if edge from $i$ to $j$, 0 otherwise);
$w_{ij}$ = weighted adjacency matrix element (trade flow value);
$\mathbf{A}$ = adjacency matrix; $\sigma_{st}$ = number of shortest
paths between nodes $s$ and $t$; $\sigma_{st}(i)$ = number of those
paths passing through $i$; $\lambda_{\max}$ = largest eigenvalue of
$\mathbf{A}$; $\mathbf{x}$ = eigenvector corresponding to
$\lambda_{\max}$; $\alpha, \beta$ = Katz parameters; $d$ = damping
factor (typically 0.85); $\mathcal{N}_i$ = neighborhood of node $i$;
$\mathcal{N}_i^{\text{in}}$ = in-neighbors of node $i$; $d(i,j)$ =
shortest path distance between nodes $i$ and $j$; $d_{jk}$ = shortest
path distance in subgraph; $r_i$ = local mass distribution within box
around node $i$; $\langle \cdot \rangle$ = ensemble average.

\acrshort{ns} & \acrlong{ns} (Overlap) & $\text{NS}(t_1, t_2) = \frac{|V_{t_1} \cap V_{t_2}|}{|V_{t_1} \cup V_{t_2}|}$ & Fraction of countries active in both time periods/layers; measures stability \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{es} & \acrlong{es} (Overlap) & $\text{ES}(t_1, t_2) = \frac{|E_{t_1} \cap E_{t_2}|}{|E_{t_1} \cup E_{t_2}|}$ & Fraction of trade links present in both layers; measures relationship persistence \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{pd} & \acrlong{pd} & $\text{PD}(t_1, t_2) = \frac{\text{cov}(\mathbf{k}_{t_1}, \mathbf{k}_{t_2})}{\sigma_{k_{t_1}} \sigma_{k_{t_2}}}$ & Linear correlation of node degrees across layers; assesses structural similarity \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{sd} & \acrlong{sd} & $\text{SD}(t_1, t_2) = 1 - \frac{6 \sum_i (R_{i,t_1} - R_{i,t_2})^2}{n(n^2-1)}$ & Rank correlation of node degrees across layers; robust to outliers \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{sp} & \acrlong{sp} & $\text{SP}(t_1, t_2) = 1 - \frac{1}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i \neq j} \frac{|d_{ij}^{t_1} - d_{ij}^{t_2}|}{\max(d_{ij}^{t_1}, d_{ij}^{t_2})}$ & Normalized distance between shortest path matrices; measures topological evolution \\

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\textbf{Notation:} $t_1, t_2$ = two time periods or network layers;
$V_t$ = set of nodes (countries) in layer $t$; $E_t$ = set of edges
(trade links) in layer $t$; $|\cdot|$ = cardinality (size) of set;
$\mathbf{k}_t$ = vector of node degrees in layer $t$;
$\text{cov}(\cdot, \cdot)$ = covariance; $\sigma_{k_t}$ = standard
deviation of degrees in layer $t$; $R_{i,t}$ = rank of node $i$'s degree
in layer $t$; $n$ = number of common nodes; $d_{ij}^t$ = shortest path
distance between nodes $i$ and $j$ in layer $t$.

\acrshort{dens} & \acrlong{dens} & $\text{Dens} = \frac{|E|}{N(N-1)}$ & Proportion of actual to possible trade links; measures network completeness \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{assort} & \acrlong{assort} & $\text{Assort} = \frac{\sum_{ij} (a_{ij} - k_i k_j / 2|E|)(k_i - \bar{k})(k_j - \bar{k})}{\sum_i k_i (k_i - \bar{k})^2}$ & Tendency of similar-degree nodes to connect; positive indicates homophily \\
\addlinespace

Trace & Trace & $\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{ii}$ & Represents the total volume of self-loops. It captures the extent of domestic or intra-industial transactions within the network. \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{dzi} & \acrlong{dzi} & $\text{DZI} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (\text{DCI}_{\max} - \text{DCI}_i)}{(N-1)^2}$ & Variation in in-degrees; high values indicate import concentration \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{dzo} & \acrlong{dzo} & $\text{DZO} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (\text{DCO}_{\max} - \text{DCO}_i)}{(N-1)^2}$ & Variation in out-degrees; high values indicate export concentration \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{bz} & \acrlong{bz} & $\text{BZ} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (\text{BC}_{\max} - \text{BC}_i)}{(N-1)(N-2)/2}$ & Variation in betweenness; high values indicate reliance on key intermediaries \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{pz} & \acrlong{pz} & $\text{PZ} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (\text{EC}_{\max} - \text{EC}_i)}{\max(\sum_{i=1}^{N} (\text{EC}_{\max} - \text{EC}_i))}$ & Variation in eigenvector centrality; measures dominance hierarchy \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{hz} & \acrlong{hz} & $\text{HZ} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (H_{\max} - H_i)}{(N-1)(N-2)}$ where $H_i = \sum_{j \neq i} \frac{1}{d(i,j)}$ & Variation in harmonic centrality; assesses accessibility inequality \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{prz} & \acrlong{prz} & $\text{PRZ} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (\text{PRC}_{\max} - \text{PRC}_i)}{\frac{N-1}{N}}$ & Variation in PageRank; measures influence concentration \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{mod} & (Leiden's) \acrlong{mod} & $\text{MOD} = \frac{1}{2|E|} \sum_{ij} \left(a_{ij} - \frac{k_i k_j}{2|E|}\right) \delta(c_i, c_j)$ & Strength of community structure; high values indicate regional trade blocs \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{trans} & \acrlong{trans} & $\text{Trans} = \frac{3 \times \text{number of triangles}}{\text{number of connected triples}}$ & Global clustering coefficient; measures triplet closure tendency \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{gle} & \acrlong{gle} & $\text{GLE} = \frac{1}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i \neq j} \frac{1}{d(i,j)}$ & Average inverse shortest path length; measures network-wide connectivity \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{ale} & \acrlong{ale} & $\text{ALE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \text{LEV}_i$ & Mean of local efficiencies; measures robustness to local disruptions \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{avpl} & \acrlong{avpl} & $\text{AVPL} = \frac{1}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i \neq j} d(i,j)$ & Mean shortest path distance; measures typical separation between countries \\
\addlinespace


\acrshort{mot} & 3-\acrlong{mot}s & $\text{MOT}_m = \frac{n_m}{\sum_{m'} n_{m'}}$ & Frequency of 3-node subgraph pattern $m$; reveals local structural motifs \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{rres} & \acrlong{rres} & $\text{RRes} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{S_i}{N}$ & Area under size-of-largest-component curve during random removal \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{sres} & \acrlong{sres} & $\text{SRes} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{S_i^*}{N}$ & Area under curve during targeted removal (by centrality); assesses vulnerability \\
\addlinespace

\acrshort{fdim} & \acrlong{fdim} & $\text{FDim} = -\frac{d \ln N_B(l_B)}{d \ln l_B}$ & Self-similarity exponent from box-covering; characterises scale-free structure \\
\addlinespace

LL\_m1 & Mean of \acrlong{ll} & LL\_m1  $=\mu_{LL}= \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \text{LL}_i$ & Average heterogeneity of local structures; indicates overall irregularity \\
\addlinespace

LL\_m2 & Stdandard Deviation of \acrlong{ll} & LL\_m2$=\sigma_{LL}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (\text{LL}_i - \mu_{LL}^2}$ & Dispersion of local heterogeneities; measures structural diversity \\
\addlinespace

LL\_m3 & Skewness of \acrlong{ll} & LL\_m3 $=\gamma_{LL}= \frac{1}{N \sigma_{LL}^3} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (\text{LL}_i - \mu_{LL})^3$ & Asymmetry of lacunarity distribution; detects concentration patterns \\
\addlinespace

LL\_m4 & Kurtosis of \acrlong{ll} & LL\_m4 $=\kappa_{LL} = \frac{1}{N \sigma_{LL}^4} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (\text{LL}_i - \mu_{LL})^4$ & Tail heaviness of lacunarity distribution; identifies extreme heterogeneity \\

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\textbf{Notation:} $|E|$ = number of edges; $k_i$ = degree of node $i$;
$\bar{k}$ = average degree;
$\text{DCI}_{\max}, \text{DCO}_{\max}, \text{BC}_{\max}, \text{EC}_{\max}, \text{PRC}_{\max}$
= maximum values of respective centralities; $H_i$ = harmonic centrality
of node $i$; $c_i$ = community assignment of node $i$;
$\delta(c_i, c_j)$ = Kronecker delta (1 if $c_i = c_j$, 0 otherwise);
$E_{>k}$ = number of edges among nodes with degree $> k$; $N_{>k}$ =
number of nodes with degree $> k$; $n_m$ = count of motif $m$; $S_i$ =
size of largest connected component after removing $i$ nodes; $S_i^*$ =
size during targeted removal; $N_B(l_B)$ = number of boxes of size $l_B$
needed to cover network.
