\textbf{Gravity Model Coefficients Context:}

\begin{description}
    \item[Distance dependence ($\beta_{\text{dist}}$):] Reflected in \gls{avpl}, \gls{gle}, \gls{ale}, \gls{ecc}, \gls{sp} — network measures of separation and efficiency capture the role of geographic/economic distance. 
    \item[Economic mass - Exporter ($\beta_{\text{GDP}_i}$):] Reflected in \gls{sco}, \gls{dco}, \gls{hc}, \gls{prc} — measures of export capacity and influence capture sender country economic role.
    \item[Economic mass - Importer ($\beta_{\text{GDP}_j}$):] Reflected in \gls{sci}, \gls{dci}, \gls{ac} — measures of import capacity and authority capture receiver country economic role.
    \item[Structural heterogeneity:] \gls{fdim}, \gls{ll} moments — fractal and lacunarity measures capture scale-free and hierarchical properties that may modulate gravity coefficients over time. Whereas, reflected in MOD, Assortativity, \gls{es}, \gls{ns} — community structure and similarity measures capture institutional and political economy factors.
\end{description}

\textbf{Research Question Context:} Time-varying gravity coefficients
may be driven by or correlated with changes in network topology. For
instance:

\begin{itemize}
    \item Increasing LL\_m1 or LL\_m2 (greater heterogeneity) may correlate with changing $\beta_{\text{dist}}$ as countries adopt diverse strategies.
    \item Rising \gls{mod} may correspond to decreasing FTA coefficients within blocs and increasing border effects between blocs.
    \item Changes in \gls{fdim} may signal structural phase transitions affecting all gravity coefficients.
    \item Granger causality tests can establish whether network indicators predict changes in gravity coefficients or vice versa, addressing endogeneity.
\end{itemize}

## Pattern recognition with network-based dimensionality analysis {#sec:gnda}

The employed \gls{gnda} [@kosztyan2024generalized] provides a robust
framework for clustering high-dimensional time series data, particularly
suited for scenarios with limited observations but numerous
variables—characteristic of retail network data with multiple products
and sectors.

\gls{gnda} addresses the fundamental challenge of determining the
optimal number of \glspl{lv} in \gls{hdlss} datasets. Unlike traditional
methods such as \gls{pca} or \gls{pfa}, which often over- or
underestimate the number of factors, \gls{gnda} leverages network
science and modularity-based community detection to identify natural
groupings of time series characteristics.

The methodology transforms the correlation structure of variables into a
network representation. Let
$\mathbf{Z} = [\mathbf{z}_1, \mathbf{z}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{z}_m]$ denote
the standardized time series matrix with $n$ observations and $m$
variables, where each $\mathbf{z}_i$ represents a standardized time
series:

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{z}_i = \frac{\mathbf{v}_i - \mu_{\mathbf{v}_i}}{\sigma_{\mathbf{v}_i}}
\end{equation}

The similarity graph $G(\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E}, \mathcal{W})$ is
constructed where nodes $i \in \mathcal{V}$ represent variables, edges
$(i,j) \in \mathcal{E}$ encode relationships, and weights
$w_{i,j} \in \mathcal{W}$ quantify similarity. For time series
clustering, the squared correlation $r_{i,j}^2$ serves as the similarity
measure, though distance correlation or other metrics may be employed
depending on the data structure.

Community detection partitions the graph into $N$ modules
$C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_N$ by maximizing the modularity function:

\begin{equation}
M = \frac{1}{2L}\sum_{i,j}\left(r_{i,j} - \gamma \hat{r}_{i,j}\right)\delta(C_i, C_j)
\end{equation}

where $L$ is the total edge weight, $\hat{r}_{i,j}$ represents the
expected weight under a null model, $\gamma$ is the resolution
parameter, and $\delta(C_i, C_j) = 1$ if nodes $i$ and $j$ belong to the
same community, zero otherwise.

For each identified module $C_I$, the corresponding latent variable is
constructed as a weighted combination of standardized time series using
\gls{ec} values as weights:

\begin{equation}
LV_I = \frac{\sum_{i \in C_I} c_i \mathbf{z}_i}{\sum_{i \in C_I} c_i}
\end{equation}

where $c_i$ denotes the eigenvector centrality of node $i$. The \gls{ec}
is defined through the dominant eigenvector of the adjacency matrix
$\mathbf{A}$:

\begin{equation}
c_k = \frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{l \in G} a_{k,l} c_l
\end{equation}

where $\lambda$ is the largest eigenvalue. This centrality measure
provides a natural interpretation analogous to factor loadings in
traditional factor analysis, with higher values indicating greater
importance within the cluster.

The critical advantage of \gls{gnda} for time series clustering lies in
its automated determination of the number of clusters through modularity
optimization, eliminating the subjective specification required by most
dimensionality reduction techniques. The method performs robustly even
when $n \ll m$, as demonstrated on simulated block matrices where GNDA
consistently identified the correct number of latent variables while PCA
and PFA frequently failed.

The resulting latent time series $LV_I$ represents the characteristic
temporal pattern of cluster $I$, capturing the common dynamics shared by
its constituent series. These cluster-level time series can be directly
utilized for forecasting, providing aggregate predictions that reflect
the collective behaviour of related variables. The EVC-weighted
aggregation ensures that more central (representative) series contribute
proportionally more to the latent variable, yielding a robust
characterisation of cluster dynamics.

## Forecastings {#sec:forecast}

### Traditional and ARIMA and Bayesian ARIMA Models {#sec:arima}

Let $y_t \in \mathbb{R}$ denote a univariate time series observed for
$t = 1,\ldots,T$. With the lag operator $L$, $L y_t = y_{t-1}$, an
ARIMA(p,d,q) model can be written in compact lag-polynomial form as
\begin{equation}
\phi(L)\,(1-L)^d\,y_t \;=\; c \;+\; \theta(L)\,\varepsilon_t,
\qquad
\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),
\label{eq:arima}
\end{equation} where $\phi(L)=1-\phi_1 L-\cdots-\phi_p L^p$ and
$\theta(L)=1+\theta_1 L+\cdots+\theta_q L^q$ enforce, respectively,
stationarity (roots of $\phi$ outside the unit circle) and invertibility
(roots of $\theta$ outside the unit circle). The operator $(1-L)^d$
encodes $d$-fold differencing. In levels, \eqref{eq:arima} may be
equivalently written as \begin{equation}
(1-L)^d y_t \;=\; \mu \;+\; \sum_{i=1}^p \phi_i\, (1-L)^d y_{t-i} \;+\; \varepsilon_t + \sum_{j=1}^q \theta_j\,\varepsilon_{t-j},
\label{eq:arima_levels}
\end{equation} with an appropriate intercept $\mu$ (linked to $c$ once
differencing is expanded).

\gls{mle} under Gaussian innovations proceeds by maximizing the exact
Gaussian likelihood of the innovation sequence
$\{\varepsilon_t(\theta)\}$ implied by \eqref{eq:arima}:
\begin{equation}
\ell(\theta; y_{1:T}) \;=\; -\frac{T}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) \;-\; \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{t=1}^T \varepsilon_t(\theta)^2,
\label{eq:lik}
\end{equation} where
$\theta=(\mu,\phi_1,\dots,\phi_p,\theta_1,\dots,\theta_q,\sigma^2)$ and
the innovations are computed via the innovations algorithm or an
equivalent state-space (Kalman filter) representation. Under regularity,
$\widehat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}$ is consistent and asymptotically normal,
but for short samples the sampling variability of
$\widehat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}$ may be substantial, and model-order
uncertainty $(p,d,q)$ can materially affect inference and prediction.

Bayesian \gls{arima}. A Bayesian specification places a prior density
$\pi(\theta)$ over the parameter vector $\theta$, truncated to the
stationarity/invertibility region. The posterior is \begin{equation}
p(\theta \mid y_{1:T}) \;\propto\; L(\theta; y_{1:T})\,\pi(\theta),
\label{eq:posterior}
\end{equation} where $L(\theta; y_{1:T})=\exp\{\ell(\theta; y_{1:T})\}$
is the Gaussian likelihood \eqref{eq:lik}. Typical weakly informative
choices include Gaussian priors on
$(\mu,\phi_1,\dots,\phi_p,\theta_1,\dots,\theta_q)$ (with transforms
enforcing the root constraints, e.g. via partial autocorrelations) and
inverse-gamma or half-t/half-Cauchy priors for $\sigma^2$. Posterior
inference is obtained by \gls{mcmc} (e.g., Metropolis–Hastings,
Gibbs-within-Metropolis, or HMC/NUTS).

A key advantage for short time series is that Bayesian inference
integrates parameter and model-order uncertainty instead of conditioning
on a single point estimate or order. The $h$-step posterior predictive
distribution is \begin{equation}
p(y_{T+h}\mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \int p\!\left(y_{T+h}\mid \theta, y_{1:T}\right)\, p(\theta\mid y_{1:T})\, d\theta,
\label{eq:ppd}
\end{equation} which averages forecasts over the posterior of $\theta$;
numerically, \eqref{eq:ppd} is approximated by Monte Carlo averages of
conditional \gls{arima} forecasts across MCMC draws of $\theta$. This
automatically widens (and often better calibrates) predictive intervals
when $T$ is small.

Conjugate special case (AR regression). When $q=0$ and $d=0$, AR($p$)
can be treated as a Gaussian regression \begin{equation}
y_t \;=\; \mu + \phi^\top y_{t-1:t-p} + \varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),
\label{eq:ar_reg}
\end{equation} with $y_{t-1:t-p}=(y_{t-1},\dots,y_{t-p})^\top$. Using a
Normal–Inverse-Gamma prior \begin{equation}
(\phi,\mu)\mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(m_0,\,\sigma^2 V_0\right), 
\qquad \sigma^2 \sim \mathrm{IG}(a_0,b_0),
\end{equation} yields closed-form posteriors \begin{eqnarray}
V_n &=& \left(V_0^{-1} + X^\top X\right)^{-1}, 
\qquad 
m_n \;=\; V_n\left(V_0^{-1} m_0 + X^\top y\right),\\
a_n &=& a_0 + \frac{n}{2},
\qquad
b_n \;=\; b_0 + \frac{1}{2}\left(y^\top y + m_0^\top V_0^{-1} m_0 - m_n^\top V_n^{-1} m_n\right),
\end{eqnarray} where $X$ collects the lag regressors and intercept, and
$n$ is the effective sample. This highlights Bayesian shrinkage: with
short $n$, $(m_0,V_0)$ regularize $(\phi,\mu)$, reducing variance and
improving predictive stability.

Model comparison and order uncertainty. Bayesian model comparison across
candidate orders $(p,d,q)$ uses Bayes factors or posterior model
probabilities. The Bayes factor for model $\mathcal{M}_1$ against
$\mathcal{M}_0$ is \begin{equation}
\mathrm{BF}_{10} \;=\; \frac{m(y_{1:T}\mid \mathcal{M}_1)}{m(y_{1:T}\mid \mathcal{M}_0)}
\;=\; \frac{\int L(\theta_1;y)\,\pi(\theta_1)\,d\theta_1}{\int L(\theta_0;y)\,\pi(\theta_0)\,d\theta_0}.
\end{equation} When computing $m(\cdot)$ exactly is costly, the Schwarz
approximation gives \begin{equation}
\log \mathrm{BF}_{10} \;\approx\; -\tfrac{1}{2}\Big(\mathrm{BIC}(\mathcal{M}_1)-\mathrm{BIC}(\mathcal{M}_0)\Big),
\qquad
\mathrm{BIC}(\mathcal{M}) \;=\; -2\ell(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathcal{M}}) + k_{\mathcal{M}}\log T,
\end{equation} which is particularly convenient in short samples (stable
and fast) and coheres with classical information criteria.

Why Bayesian methods help with short series. For small $T$, (i) priors
induce shrinkage that mitigates overfitting of $\phi$ and $\theta$; (ii)
posterior predictive \eqref{eq:ppd} accounts for parameter uncertainty
that \gls{mle}-based plug-in forecasts ignore; (iii) model uncertainty
over $(p,d,q)$ can be integrated rather than decided by a single
pretest; and (iv) stationarity/invertibility constraints are enforced by
the prior support or parameter transforms. Collectively, these features
improve finite-sample calibration of uncertainty and reduce spurious
dynamics—properties that are crucial when only short annual histories
are available.

## Causality Analysis {#sec:calccaus}

### Implementation and imputation {#sec:imputation}

All three methods require complete time series. We handle missing values
via linear interpolation using the \texttt{imputeTS} package
[@moritz2017]. For each sector $j$ and variable $i$, gaps in $Y_{j,t}$
and $X_{i,j,t}$ are filled by linear interpolation between observed
neighbors, preserving temporal structure.

Each panel Granger causal test method produces an $M \times (J+1)$
matrix $\mathbf{P} = [\widehat{p}_{i,j}]$, where rows correspond to
explanatory variables, columns $1,\ldots,J$ to individual sectors, and
column $J+1$ to the pooled panel. An entry $\widehat{p}_{i,j} > 0$
indicates that variable $i$ Granger-causes sector $j$'s outcome at lag
$\widehat{p}_{i,j}$; an entry of zero indicates no detectable causality.
Comparing matrices across methods reveals robustness: relationships
detected by all three approaches are likely genuine, whereas
method-specific findings may reflect linearity assumptions (traditional
and Bayesian) or nonlinear patterns (Random Forest).

The lag estimates $\{\widehat{p}_{i,j}\}$ inform the temporal dynamics
of causal relationships, enabling time series analyses such as
impulse-response functions, forecasting models, and event studies that
respect the identified causal lags. Sector-level heterogeneity in
$\widehat{p}_{i,j}$ reveals differential adjustment speeds or
transmission mechanisms across sectors, analogous to the heterogeneity
in distance elasticities $\gamma_t^{(k)}$ discussed in the gravity model
context.

### Traditional and Bayesian Granger Causality Analysis {#sec:tradgc}

Let $y_t \in \mathbb{R}$ denote the scalar target (explained) series and
$X_t=(x_{1,t},\dots,x_{d,t})^\top \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the vector of
candidate explanatory (predictor) series observed for $t=1,\dots,T$. Fix
a maximum lag order $p\ge 1$. lag-$\ell$ values are written as
$y_{t-\ell}$ and $x_{j,t-\ell}$, and index sets over variables and lags
are finite.

We use two closely related linear formulations. The first is a full
ARX(p) model for $y_t$ involving its own lags and all X-lags:
\begin{equation}
y_t \;=\; c \;+\; \sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\phi_{\ell}\,y_{t-\ell} \;+\; \sum_{j=1}^{d}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p}\beta_{j,\ell}\,x_{j,t-\ell} \;+\; \varepsilon_t,\quad \varepsilon_t\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),
\label{eq:arx}
\end{equation}

and the second is a bivariate $VAR(p)$ for each pair $(y,x_j)$, written
with $Y_{j,t}=(y_t,\,x_{j,t})^\top$,

\begin{equation}
Y_{j,t} \;=\; a_j \;+\; \sum_{\ell=1}^{p}A_{j,\ell}\,Y_{j,t-\ell} \;+\; u_{j,t},\qquad u_{j,t}\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_j).
\label{eq:var}
\end{equation}

Classical Granger causality of $x_j \to y$ asks whether past $x_j$ helps
predict $y$ beyond $y$’s own past and (when applicable) the past of the
remaining variables in the model.

In the ARX formulation \eqref{eq:arx}, Granger non-causality of $x_j$
with respect to $y$ is the linear restriction

\begin{equation}
H_{0,j}:\;\beta_{j,1}=\cdots=\beta_{j,p}=0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_{1,j}:\;\exists\,\ell\in\{1,\dots,p\}\;\text{such that}\;\beta_{j,\ell}\neq 0.
\label{eq:h0}
\end{equation}

In the bivariate VAR formulation \eqref{eq:var}, Granger non-causality
corresponds to zeroing all coefficients of lagged $x_j$ in the
$y$-equation of $Y_{j,t}$.

We use three complementary evidential tools: (i) a classical nested
F–test; (ii) an information-criterion check via BIC; and (iii) Bayesian
validation combining Bayes factors and \gls{mcmc}-based credible
intervals. A causal link is accepted only when the pre-specified
classical significance and the Bayesian conditions jointly hold; the
information criterion serves as an additional strength-of-evidence
measure and as a basis for importance metrics.

Classical nested F–test (ARX). Let $\mathcal{M}_{\text{full}}$ be
\eqref{eq:arx} and $\mathcal{M}_{\text{red},j}$ the reduced model
obtained by removing the $p$ regressors $\{x_{j,t-\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{p}$.
Denote by $\mathrm{RSS}_{\text{full}}$ and $\mathrm{RSS}_{\text{red},j}$
the residual sum of squares, $q_j$ the number of restrictions ($=p$),
and $k_{\text{full}}$ the number of free parameters in
$\mathcal{M}_{\text{full}}$. The standard Wald/F statistic is

\begin{equation}
F_j \;=\; \frac{\big(\mathrm{RSS}_{\text{red},j}-\mathrm{RSS}_{\text{full}}\big)/q_j}{\mathrm{RSS}_{\text{full}}/(T-k_{\text{full}})}
\;\sim\; F\big(q_j,\,T-k_{\text{full}}\big)\;\;\text{under }H_{0,j}.
\label{eq:Ftest}
\end{equation}

We reject $H_{0,j}$ at level $\alpha$ when the $p$–value $p_j$ satisfies
$p_j\le \alpha$. In the bivariate VAR test, the same logic applies but
the restriction is imposed only on the y–equation of \eqref{eq:var}.

Information-criterion (BIC) check. As an information-theoretic control
that is less sensitive to finite-sample variance, we also compute the
BIC difference between the reduced and full models:

\begin{equation}
\Delta\mathrm{BIC}_j \;=\; \mathrm{BIC}(\mathcal{M}_{\text{red},j}) \;-\; \mathrm{BIC}(\mathcal{M}_{\text{full}}),
\qquad
\mathrm{BIC}(\mathcal{M}) \;=\; -2\log L(\widehat{\theta}_{\mathcal{M}})\;+\; k_{\mathcal{M}}\log T.
\label{eq:dbic}
\end{equation}

A positive $\Delta\mathrm{BIC}_j$ indicates that including the lags of
$x_j$ improves the information criterion and therefore supports
$x_j \to y$. In practice we use $\Delta\mathrm{BIC}_j$ primarily as (i)
an evidence-strength score consistent with the classical test; and (ii)
a building block for relative-importance metrics.

Expected delay (lag selection) and lag-level importance. For each
predictor $x_j$ we estimate the “dominant” delay by the lag index
achieving the largest absolute t–statistic in the unrestricted
y–equation:

\begin{equation}
\widehat{\ell}_j \;=\; \arg\max_{\ell\in\{1,\dots,p\}} \big|t_{j,\ell}\big|,
\qquad
t_{j,\ell} \;=\; \frac{\widehat{\beta}_{j,\ell}}{\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat{\beta}_{j,\ell})}.
\label{eq:expLag}
\end{equation}

If $H_{0,j}$ is not rejected (classically and Bayes-wise; see below), we
set $\widehat{\ell}_j=0$. Within-variable lag importance profiles use
$\big|t_{j,\ell}\big|$; aggregated lag importances over $\ell$ are
obtained by summation and normalization.

Relative-importance measures (random-forest–like scoring). We employ two
complementary, scale-free scores:

\begin{eqnarray}
s^{(p)}_j \;&=&\; \big[-\log_{10}(p_j)\big]\;\mathbf{1}\{p_j\le \alpha\},
\qquad
\mathsf{Imp}^{(p)}_j \;=\; \frac{s^{(p)}_j}{\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}} s^{(p)}_k},
\label{eq:impP}\\
s^{(\mathrm{BIC})}_j \;&=&\; \max\big\{0,\,\Delta\mathrm{BIC}_j\big\},
\qquad\;\;
\mathsf{Imp}^{(\mathrm{BIC})}_j \;=\; \frac{s^{(\mathrm{BIC})}_j}{\sum_{k} s^{(\mathrm{BIC})}_k},
\label{eq:impBIC}
\end{eqnarray}

\noindent where $\mathcal{S}=\{j:\,p_j\le \alpha\}$. Equation
\eqref{eq:impP} mirrors random-forest practice by assigning positive
mass only to statistically significant drivers and renormalizing their
weights to sum to 1. Equation \eqref{eq:impBIC} interprets
$\Delta\mathrm{BIC}_j$ as an information-theoretic “gain” and normalizes
the positive gains across variables. In both cases, larger values
indicate stronger evidence that $x_j$ improves predictive content for
$y$ relative to other candidates.

Choice of a strict $\alpha=0.01$ for short panels. In applied work with
relatively short annual trade panels, the number of candidate variables
and lags can be large relative to $T$. This inflates the number of
simultaneous linear restrictions tested and the chance of spurious
rejections. A stringent level $\alpha=0.01$ controls Type I error more
aggressively; under $m$ independent tests, the family-wise error rate
satisfies

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{FWER}\;\approx\; 1-(1-\alpha)^m\;\le\; m\alpha,
\end{equation}

\noindent so reducing $\alpha$ curbs the expected number of false
positives $m\alpha$ in small samples. This is particularly important
when screening many $x_j$ and lags $\ell$.

Bayesian validation: Bayes factors and \gls{mcmc} credible intervals. To
corroborate classical rejections and guard against overfitting, we
require Bayesian support in two forms.

(i) Bayes factor comparing full vs reduced models for $x_j$. Let
    $\mathcal{M}_{\text{full}}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{\text{red},j}$ be as
    above. The Bayes factor is

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{BF}_j \;=\; \frac{m\!\left(D\mid \mathcal{M}_{\text{full}}\right)}{m\!\left(D\mid \mathcal{M}_{\text{red},j}\right)}
\;=\; \frac{\displaystyle \int L(\theta_{\text{full}};D)\,\pi(\theta_{\text{full}})\,d\theta_{\text{full}}}{\displaystyle \int L(\theta_{\text{red},j};D)\,\pi(\theta_{\text{red},j})\,d\theta_{\text{red},j}},
\label{eq:bf}
\end{equation}

\noindent with $L$ the likelihood and $\pi(\cdot)$ prior densities. We
adopt the widely used threshold $\mathrm{BF}_j\ge 5$ as “substantial”
evidence for the full model. In practice we also use the BIC
approximation

\begin{equation}
\log \mathrm{BF}_j \;\approx\; \tfrac{1}{2}\Big(\mathrm{BIC}(\mathcal{M}_{\text{red},j})-\mathrm{BIC}(\mathcal{M}_{\text{full}})\Big),
\label{eq:bicapprox}
\end{equation}

\noindent which coheres with $\Delta\mathrm{BIC}_j$ and is stable on
short samples.

(ii) Posterior exclusion of zero for at least one lag of $x_j$. Under
     \eqref{eq:arx} with a proper prior $\pi(\beta,\sigma^2)$,
     \gls{mcmc} draws $\{ \beta^{(r)},\sigma^{2\,(r)}\}_{r=1}^{R}$
     target

\begin{equation}
p(\beta,\sigma^2\mid D) \;\propto\; L(\beta,\sigma^2;D)\,\pi(\beta,\sigma^2).
\end{equation}

For each $j$ we form credible intervals
$\big[\beta_{j,\ell}^{L},\,\beta_{j,\ell}^{U}\big]$ at level $1-\gamma$
(e.g., 0.95). We declare Bayesian support for $x_j \to y$ if

\begin{equation}
\exists\,\ell\in\{1,\dots,p\}\;\text{such that}\; 0 \notin \big[\beta_{j,\ell}^{L},\,\beta_{j,\ell}^{U}\big].
\label{eq:ci}
\end{equation}

Decision rule (intersection). A causal link is accepted only if
\begin{equation}
\boxed{\;p_j\le \alpha\;\;\wedge\;\;\mathrm{BF}_j\ge 5\;\;\wedge\;\;\text{\eqref{eq:ci} holds}\;}
\end{equation}

\noindent and then the expected delay $\widehat{\ell}_j$ is assigned by
\eqref{eq:expLag}; otherwise $\widehat{\ell}_j:=0$.

Causal structure among the explanatory variables. Beyond $x_j \to y$, we
characterise the internal dependence of the explanatory block X_t by
constructing a directed graph $\mathcal{G}=(V,E,W)$ on
$V=\{1,\dots,d\}$:

\begin{eqnarray}
(i\to k)\in E &\Longleftrightarrow& \text{$x_i$ Granger-causes $x_k$ (same testing logic as above)},\\
W_{ik} &=& \widehat{\ell}_{ik}\in\{1,\dots,p\}\;\;\text{(edge weight = estimated delay)},
\end{eqnarray}

\noindent with $\widehat{\ell}_{ik}$ the lag maximizing $|t|$ in the
$x_k$–equation when testing $x_i \to x_k$. This graph underpins the
interpretation of $y$–drivers by revealing potential upstream/downstream
channels among the predictors.

Short-sample regularization and implementation notes. In practice, to
stabilize estimation with short $T$ we (i) restrict $p$ via data-driven
selection or conservative caps; (ii) use information-criterion
differentials $\Delta\mathrm{BIC}_j$ to grade evidence; and (iii) in the
bivariate VAR workflow for each $x_j$ use the Granger test $p_j$ and the
standardized t–statistics to form $\widehat{\ell}_j$. The
relative-importance scores $\mathsf{Imp}^{(p)}_j$ and
$\mathsf{Imp}^{(\mathrm{BIC})}_j$ are normalized to sum to 1 across
significant variables, making them directly comparable across
specifications and akin to random-forest variable-importance magnitudes.

Finally, we note two caveats. First, all procedures above detect only
\emph{linear} Granger-causal relations; nonlinear predictive effects are
not identified by \eqref{eq:arx}–\eqref{eq:var}. Second, causal
interpretation of $x_j \to y$ can be distorted when strong causal links
exist among the predictors themselves (as reflected by $\mathcal{G}$).
In subsequent sections we address these issues by employing
random-forest models, which can flexibly capture nonlinearities and
interactions and deliver alternative, stability-oriented importance
measures that are less sensitive to linear-model misspecification.

### Random Forest-Based Granger-Like Causality Analysis {#sec:rfgc}

Let $\{y_t\}_{t=1}^n$ denote the target (explained) time series and let
$\{x_{j,t}\}_{t=1}^n$ for $j=1,\dots,p$ denote $p$ candidate explanatory
series. Fix a maximum lag $L\in\mathbb{N}$. For each time $t>L$, define
the lagged covariate blocks

\begin{equation}
u_t \;=\; \big(y_{t-1},y_{t-2},\dots,y_{t-L}\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{L}, 
\qquad
v_{j,t} \;=\; \big(x_{j,t-1},x_{j,t-2},\dots,x_{j,t-L}\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{L},
\end{equation}

and the full predictor vector

\begin{equation}
z_t \;=\; \big(u_t, v_{1,t},\dots,v_{p,t}\big)\in \mathbb{R}^{L(p+1)}.
\end{equation}

The effective sample is $\mathcal{T}=\{L+1,\dots,n\}$ after trimming the
first $L$ indices.

We consider two random-forest regression models: \begin{align*}
\text{Full model:}\quad & y_t \;=\; f(z_t) + \varepsilon_t, \\
\text{Baseline (AR) model:}\quad & y_t \;=\; g(u_t) + \eta_t,
\end{align*}

\noindent where $f$ and $g$ are fitted by random forests on their
respective features. A random-forest predictor with $B$ trees has the
form

\begin{equation}
\widehat f(z) \;=\; \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B T_b(z),
\end{equation}

\noindent where $T_b$ is the $b$-th regression tree trained on a
bootstrap sample and using feature subsampling at splits. The AR
baseline uses only $u_t$; if AR lags are disabled, the baseline reduces
to a constant (the training mean).

To estimate out-of-sample (OOS) performance without temporal leakage, we
partition $\mathcal{T}$ into $K$ contiguous folds $F_1,\dots,F_K$ of
approximately equal size. For each $f=2,\dots,K$:

\begin{equation}
\text{Train on } \bigcup_{r=1}^{f-1} F_r, \qquad \text{test on } F_f.
\end{equation}

Let $\widehat g^{(f)}$ and $\widehat f^{(f)}$ denote the baseline and
full models trained for fold $f$. Define the OOS mean squared errors
(MSEs)

\begin{equation}
\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{base}}
\;=\;
\frac{1}{N_{\text{test}}}\sum_{f=2}^K \sum_{t\in F_f}\big(y_t-\widehat g^{(f)}(u_t)\big)^2,
\qquad
\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{full}}
\;=\;
\frac{1}{N_{\text{test}}}\sum_{f=2}^K \sum_{t\in F_f}\big(y_t-\widehat f^{(f)}(z_t)\big)^2,
\end{equation}

\noindent where $N_{\text{test}}=\sum_{f=2}^K |F_f|$. Two summary
measures reported are

\begin{equation}
\Delta_{\text{rel}} \;=\; 1-\frac{\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{full}}}{\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{base}}}
\quad\text{(relative MSE reduction; Granger-style incremental predictability),}
\end{equation}

\noindent and the OOS $R^2$ against the test mean,

\begin{equation}
R^2_{\text{oos}} \;=\; 1 - \frac{\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{full}}}{\operatorname{Var}_{\text{test}}(y_t)}.
\end{equation}

Let $\mathcal{S}$ index all features in the full model: the $L$ lags of
$y$ and the $L$ lags of each $x_j$ (so $|\mathcal{S}| = L(p+1)$). For a
feature $s\in\mathcal{S}$, let $z_t^{\pi(s)}$ denote $z_t$ with the
$s$-th coordinate permuted independently across the (out-of-bag or
held-out) evaluation set.

The permutation (Breiman) importance for feature $s$ is the OOB increase
in prediction error when $s$ is permuted:

\begin{equation}
\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}_{\text{perm}}(s)
\;=\;
\frac{1}{N_{\text{OOB}}}\sum_{t\in\text{OOB}}
\Big[
\big(y_t - \widehat f(z_t^{\pi(s)})\big)^2
-
\big(y_t - \widehat f(z_t)\big)^2
\Big].
\end{equation}

In practice, the average is taken over OOB predictions aggregated across
trees; positive values indicate that permuting $s$ harms accuracy (thus
$s$ is important). Small negative values can occur due to sampling
noise.

Alternatively, one may use the total decrease in node impurity (variance
for regression) attributed to $s$ and accumulated over all splits on $s$
across all trees:

\begin{equation}
\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}_{\text{imp}}(s)
\;=\;
\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B
\sum_{\text{splits } \nu \text{ on } s}
\Big[
\operatorname{Var}(\text{parent}_\nu)
-
\frac{n_L}{n_P}\operatorname{Var}(\text{left}_\nu)
-
\frac{n_R}{n_P}\operatorname{Var}(\text{right}_\nu)
\Big],
\end{equation}

\noindent where $(n_P,n_L,n_R)$ are sample sizes at the
parent/left/right nodes.

In the implementation, importances are computed once by refitting the
full model $\widehat f$ on all available lagged observations
$\{(z_t,y_t): t\in\mathcal{T}\}$ and extracting
$\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}(s)$ for each feature $s$ from the trained
forest.

Index the lag-$\ell$ feature of variable $x_j$ by $(j,\ell)$,
$\ell=1,\dots,L$. Define:

\begin{equation}
\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}(j,\ell) \;=\; \widehat{\operatorname{VI}}\big(s=(j,\ell)\big), 
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}_j \;=\; \sum_{\ell=1}^L \widehat{\operatorname{VI}}(j,\ell)
\quad\text{(variable-level importance)}.
\end{equation}

A relative variable importance (over $X$ only) is obtained via
normalization

\begin{equation}
\widetilde{\operatorname{VI}}_j
\;=\;
\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}_j}{\sum_{m=1}^p \widehat{\operatorname{VI}}_m},
\end{equation}

\noindent whenever the denominator is positive (otherwise normalization
is left undefined). Analogously, the global importance of lag $\ell$
across all $X$ variables is

\begin{equation}
\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}^{\text{lag}}(\ell)
\;=\;
\sum_{j=1}^p \widehat{\operatorname{VI}}(j,\ell),
\qquad
\widetilde{\operatorname{VI}}^{\text{lag}}(\ell)
\;=\;
\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}^{\text{lag}}(\ell)}
{\sum_{r=1}^L \widehat{\operatorname{VI}}^{\text{lag}}(r)}.
\end{equation}

Importances for the autoregressive lags of $y$ are computed in the same
way using the features $\{y_{t-\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^L$.

For each explanatory variable $x_j$, the most likely (dominant) lag is
chosen as the lag with the largest importance:

\begin{equation}
\widehat{\ell}_j \;\in\; \arg\max_{\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}} \widehat{\operatorname{VI}}(j,\ell),
\end{equation}

with ties broken in favor of the smallest lag. A variable-level drop
rule declares \`\`no Granger-style predictability'' if the largest
lag-importance fails to exceed a nonnegative threshold $\tau_0$:

\begin{equation}
\max_{\ell} \widehat{\operatorname{VI}}(j,\ell) \;\le\; \tau_0
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\text{drop } x_j \text{ and set expected lag } \widehat{\tau}_j=0,
\end{equation}

\noindent otherwise $\widehat{\tau}_j=\widehat{\ell}_j$. In the
implementation, $\tau_0=0$ by default (appropriate for permutation
importance where negative values can occur). For additional
interpretability, a within-variable \`\`lag share'' is also reported:

\begin{equation}
\text{lag\_share}_j
\;=\;
\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}(j,\widehat{\ell}_j)}
{\sum_{\ell=1}^L \widehat{\operatorname{VI}}(j,\ell)}
\quad \text{(defined when the denominator is positive)}.
\end{equation}

The procedure operationalizes Granger causality in a predictive sense:
$x_j$ is said to Granger-cause $y$ (at some lag) if including
$\{x_{j,t-\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^L$ alongside $y$'s own lags improves the OOS
prediction of $y_t$, as evidenced by (i) a positive and dominant
$\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}(j,\ell)$ for some $\ell$, and/or (ii) a
reduction in OOS error relative to the AR baseline
($\Delta_{\text{rel}}>0$). This is not a statement of structural
(interventional) causality; it detects incremental predictability
conditional on past information.

\subsection*{The steps of Random-Based Causality Analysis}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Build the lagged dataset $\{(z_t,y_t)\}_{t\in\mathcal{T}}$ for a chosen $L$.
\item Blocked CV: for $f=2,\dots,K$, train $\widehat g^{(f)}$ on $u_t$ and $\widehat f^{(f)}$ on $z_t$ using $\bigcup_{r<f}F_r$; score OOS on $F_f$ to compute $\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{base}}$, $\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{full}}$, $\Delta_{\text{rel}}$, and $R^2_{\text{oos}}$.
\item Fit the final full forest $\widehat f$ on all $\{(z_t,y_t)\}$ and compute feature importances $\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}(s)$ (permutation or impurity).
\item Aggregate to $\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}_j$, $\widetilde{\operatorname{VI}}_j$, $\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}(j,\ell)$, and $\widehat{\operatorname{VI}}^{\text{lag}}(\ell)$; select expected lags $\widehat{\tau}_j$ with the drop rule based on $\tau_0$.
\end{enumerate}

It should be noted that, permutation importances can be slightly
negative; the default drop threshold $\tau_0=0$ treats such cases as
non-evidence for predictability. Group-level normalizations (e.g.,
relative variable importances across $X$) are performed only when the
relevant totals are positive. Blocked CV (growing training window)
avoids look-ahead bias and mimics realistic forecasting evaluation.

A variable $x_j$ is declared to exhibit RF-based Granger causality to $y$ 
if and only if:
\begin{equation}
\boxed{
\widehat{\text{VI}}_j > 0 \;\;\wedge\;\; 
\max_{\ell} \widehat{\text{VI}}(j,\ell) > 
\max_{k,\ell} \widehat{\text{VI}}(\widetilde{x}_{j,\ell}^{(k)})
}
\label{eq:rf_decision}
\end{equation}
where the first condition ensures positive aggregate importance and the 
second requires the variable's best lag to exceed all shadow feature 
importances. The expected lag is then set to 
$\widehat{\tau}_j = \arg\max_{\ell} \widehat{\text{VI}}(j,\ell)$.

## Panel version of Granger-causality tests {#sec:pgc}

Let $Y_{j,t}$ denote the dependent variable for sector $j$ in period
$t$, where $j \in \{1,\ldots,J\}$ and $t \in \{1,\ldots,T\}$. Let
$X_{i,j,t}$ represent explanatory variable $i$ for sector $j$ in period
$t$, where $i \in \{1,\ldots,M\}$. The panel Granger causality framework
tests whether past values of $X_{i,j,t}$ contain information that helps
predict $Y_{j,t}$ beyond what is already captured by past values of
$Y_{j,t}$ itself.

### Traditional Panel Granger Causality {#sec:tpgc}

Following the seminal work of @granger1969, Granger causality in a panel
context [@holtz-eakin1988; @dumitrescu2012] is assessed by comparing a
*restricted* autoregressive model against an *unrestricted* model that
includes lagged values of the candidate causal variable.

For each sector $j$ and explanatory variable $i$, the restricted model
is:

\begin{equation}
Y_{j,t} = \alpha_{j} + \sum_{\ell=1}^{p} \beta_{\ell,j} Y_{j,t-\ell} + \varepsilon_{j,t},
\label{eq:granger_restricted}
\end{equation}

\noindent where $p$ is the lag order, $\alpha_{j}$ is a sector-specific
intercept, and $\varepsilon_{j,t}$ is an error term. The unrestricted
model augments \eqref{eq:granger_restricted} with lagged values of
$X_{i,j,t}$:

\begin{equation}
Y_{j,t} = \alpha_{j} + \sum_{\ell=1}^{p} \beta_{\ell,j} Y_{j,t-\ell} + \sum_{\ell=1}^{p} \delta_{\ell,i,j} X_{i,j,t-\ell} + u_{j,t}.
\label{eq:granger_unrestricted}
\end{equation}

\noindent The null hypothesis
$H_0\colon \delta_{1,i,j} = \delta_{2,i,j} = \cdots = \delta_{p,i,j} = 0$
states that $X_{i,j,t}$ does \textit{not} Granger-cause $Y_{j,t}$. This
hypothesis is tested using a Wald test (F-test) that compares the
residual sum of squares from \eqref{eq:granger_restricted} and
\eqref{eq:granger_unrestricted}:

\begin{equation}
F_{i,j,p} = \frac{(\text{RSS}_{\text{restricted}} - \text{RSS}_{\text{unrestricted}})/p}{\text{RSS}_{\text{unrestricted}}/(T - 2p - 1)},
\label{eq:granger_ftest}
\end{equation}

\noindent where RSS denotes the residual sum of squares. Under the null
and standard regularity conditions, $F_{i,j,p} \sim F(p, T - 2p - 1)$.
Rejection at significance level $\alpha$ (e.g., $\alpha = 0.01$)
provides evidence that $X_{i,j,t}$ Granger-causes $Y_{j,t}$ at lag $p$.

For pooled (panel-wide) inference, we stack observations across sectors
and estimate a panel model with sector fixed effects:

\begin{equation}
Y_{j,t} = \alpha_{j} + \sum_{\ell=1}^{p} \beta_{\ell} Y_{j,t-\ell} + \sum_{\ell=1}^{p} \delta_{\ell,i} X_{i,j,t-\ell} + u_{j,t},
\label{eq:granger_panel}
\end{equation}

\noindent where the fixed effects $\alpha_{j}$ control for unobserved
sector-specific heterogeneity. The panel Wald test then evaluates
whether $\delta_{1,i} = \cdots = \delta_{p,i} = 0$ across all sectors
jointly [@dumitrescu2012].

*Lag selection.* We test lag orders $p \in \{1,\ldots,p_{\max}\}$
sequentially and report the *minimum* lag $\widehat{p}_{i,j}$ at which
the null is rejected. If no lag achieves significance, we set
$\widehat{p}_{i,j} = 0$, indicating no detectable Granger causality. The
resulting matrix $\mathbf{P} = [\widehat{p}_{i,j}]_{M \times (J+1)}$
summarizes the causal structure: columns $1,\ldots,J$ correspond to
individual sectors, and column $J+1$ to the pooled panel.

### Bayesian Panel Granger causality {#sec:bpgc}

The Bayesian approach replaces hypothesis testing with model comparison
via Bayes factors [@koop2010; @koop2013]. For each lag $p$, we compute
the marginal likelihoods of the restricted model $\mathcal{M}^{(R)}_p$
(equation \eqref{eq:granger_restricted}) and the unrestricted model
$\mathcal{M}^{(U)}_p$ (equation \eqref{eq:granger_unrestricted}) using
\gls{jzs} priors on the regression coefficients [@liang2008;
@rouder2012]. The Bayes factor in favor of the unrestricted model is:

\begin{equation}
\text{BF}_{i,j,p} = \frac{p(\mathbf{Y}_j \mid \mathcal{M}^{(U)}_p)}{p(\mathbf{Y}_j \mid \mathcal{M}^{(R)}_p)},
\label{eq:bayes_factor}
\end{equation}

\noindent where $\mathbf{Y}_j = (Y_{j,p+1},\ldots,Y_{j,T})^\top$ is the
observed data vector for sector $j$. Larger values of
$\text{BF}_{i,j,p}$ indicate stronger evidence that including lagged
$X_{i,j,t}$ improves predictions of $Y_{j,t}$.

Following established conventions [@kass1995; @jeffreys1961], we
interpret the strength of evidence as: \begin{align*}
\text{BF}_{i,j,p} \geq 3 &\quad \text{positive evidence for Granger causality,} \\
\text{BF}_{i,j,p} \geq 5 &\quad \text{strong evidence (default threshold),} \\
\text{BF}_{i,j,p} \geq 10 &\quad \text{very strong evidence,} \\
\text{BF}_{i,j,p} \geq 30 &\quad \text{decisive evidence.}
\end{align*}

\noindent For each explanatory variable $i$ and sector $j$, we compute
$\text{BF}_{i,j,p}$ for all $p \in \{1,\ldots,p_{\max}\}$ and report the
minimum lag $\widehat{p}_{i,j}$ satisfying
$\text{BF}_{i,j,p} \geq \text{BF}_{\min}$ (with $\text{BF}_{\min} = 5$
by default). If no lag meets this criterion, we set
$\widehat{p}_{i,j} = 0$.

For the pooled panel, we extend \eqref{eq:granger_panel} by treating
sector fixed effects $\alpha_j$ as random effects and computing Bayes
factors that integrate over the posterior distribution of
$(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_J)$. This accounts for cross-sectional
heterogeneity while assessing Granger causality at the panel level.

The Bayesian framework avoids multiple-testing issues inherent in
sequential hypothesis testing and provides a continuous measure of
evidence strength. It naturally incorporates prior information and
yields probabilistic statements about model plausibility rather than
binary reject/fail-to-reject decisions.

### Random Forest Panel Granger Causality {#sec:rfpgc}

\gls{ml} methods can capture nonlinear Granger causality that linear
models may miss. We employ Random Forests [@breiman2001], a
nonparametric ensemble method, combined with a Boruta-style variable
selection procedure [@kursa2010] to identify relevant lagged predictors.

For lag $p$, we construct a training dataset: \begin{equation}
\mathcal{D}_{j,p} = \bigl\{ (Y_{j,t-1},\ldots,Y_{j,t-p}, X_{i,j,t-1},\ldots,X_{i,j,t-p}; Y_{j,t}) \bigr\}_{t=p+1}^{T}.
\label{eq:rf_data}
\end{equation}

\noindent A Random Forest $\mathcal{F}_{j,p}$ is trained to predict
$Y_{j,t}$ from the lagged features
$\{Y_{j,t-\ell}, X_{i,j,t-\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^p$ via an ensemble of
decision trees. Each tree is grown on a bootstrap sample, and at each
node, a random subset of features is considered for splitting. The final
prediction is the average (for regression) over all trees
[@breiman2001].

\textit{Variable importance and shadow features} To assess whether the
lagged $X_{i,j,t-\ell}$ variables contribute meaningful predictive
power, we implement a Boruta-inspired shadow feature approach
[@kursa2010]:

\begin{enumerate}
\item For each feature $Z \in \{Y_{j,t-1},\ldots,Y_{j,t-p}, X_{i,j,t-1},\ldots,X_{i,j,t-p}\}$, create $K$ \textit{shadow features} $\widetilde{Z}^{(1)},\ldots,\widetilde{Z}^{(K)}$ by randomly permuting the values of $Z$ across observations. Shadow features have no true predictive relationship with $Y_{j,t}$ by construction.
\item Train the Random Forest on the augmented dataset that includes both original and shadow features.
\item Compute permutation-based variable importance [@breiman2001] for each feature. Permutation importance measures the increase in prediction error when the feature's values are randomly shuffled, quantifying its contribution to model accuracy.
\item For explanatory variable $i$, compute the average importance of its lagged features:
\begin{equation}
I_{i,j,p} = \frac{1}{p} \sum_{\ell=1}^{p} \text{Imp}(X_{i,j,t-\ell}),
\label{eq:rf_importance}
\end{equation}
where $\text{Imp}(X_{i,j,t-\ell})$ denotes the permutation importance of $X_{i,j,t-\ell}$.
\item Compute the maximum shadow importance:

\begin{equation}
I^{\text{shadow}}_{\max,j,p} = \max_{\ell,k} \text{Imp}\bigl(\widetilde{X}_{i,j,t-\ell}^{(k)}\bigr).
\label{eq:rf_shadow_max}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

\noindent Variable $X_{i,j,t}$ is deemed to Granger-cause $Y_{j,t}$ at
lag $p$ if and only if $I_{i,j,p} > I^{\text{shadow}}_{\max,j,p}$---that
is, its importance exceeds that of all shadow (purely random) features.

\textit{Lag selection.} We compute $I_{i,j,p}$ and
$I^{\text{shadow}}_{\max,j,p}$ for all $p \in \{1,\ldots,p_{\max}\}$ and
identify the lag $\widehat{p}_{i,j}$ at which $I_{i,j,p}$ is maximized
\textit{and} satisfies
$I_{i,j,\widehat{p}_{i,j}} > I^{\text{shadow}}_{\max,j,\widehat{p}_{i,j}}$.
If no lag meets this condition, we set $\widehat{p}_{i,j} = 0$,
indicating that $X_{i,j,t}$ does not provide predictive power beyond
random chance.

For the pooled panel, we stack observations across sectors and include
sector indicators as categorical features in the Random Forest. The same
shadow-feature procedure is applied to the pooled data, yielding a
panel-level lag estimate $\widehat{p}_{i,J+1}$.

The Random Forest approach accommodates nonlinear and interaction
effects without prespecification, is robust to outliers and
distributional violations, and naturally handles high-dimensional
predictor spaces. The shadow-feature method provides a principled
threshold for distinguishing signal from noise, akin to the Boruta
algorithm's strategy for all-relevant feature selection [@kursa2010].
